stories.story:
A nurse who was deputy manager at a care home in Mold, Flintshire, has been struck off the nursing register after a regulatory hearing found she had exploited a vulnerable elderly resident. Rebecca Louise Burwood was found by the Nursing and Midwifery Council to have abused a position of trust and power over the 99-year-old between 2017 and 2023. The woman had no family nearby and depended on Burwood for company.

The hearing heard that more than £370,000 left the resident's bank account over five years, with about £160,000 taken through large cash withdrawals at cash machines. Burwood also became the resident's lasting power of attorney and was involved in having the ownership of the woman's £400,000 home transferred to her. Evidence suggested the money was used for house improvements, utility bills and council tax, and there were allegations it funded cosmetic surgery. The resident also paid for a £20,000 car and a £9,000 campervan.

Burwood said the withdrawals were weekly cash donations to charities, but she kept no records. The panel did not accept this account in full. It found she had told the woman she could not go on outings unless she could access her money, and a colleague reported hearing her say she would return the money and asking the resident to 'sign here'. The bank had frozen the account over spending concerns, and police investigated, though the woman did not want further action.

The panel described Burwood's behaviour as a sustained and calculated course of conduct that was morally reprehensible. It also found she had dishonestly failed to tell her employer about the power of attorney. Burwood said she regretted her actions and saw the resident as a grandmother figure. The care home said it fully supported the regulator's decision. The case highlights the risks of financial abuse of vulnerable care residents, and the regulator's ruling is the outcome of a fitness-to-practise process.

stories.story:
Police in South Africa have arrested a pastor and his wife after officials found about 200 people, some of them in chains, at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in Mpumalanga province in the north-east of the country. The facility was operated from a church and was discovered in a raid by officials on Thursday.

Authorities described what they found as gross inhumane conditions. Some patients had sores over their bodies and others were chained to one another. A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were among those held in the same rooms as adults. The couple had told officials they were housing 60 people, but more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women. Many were believed to be drug users, and some had been there for a long time.

The couple have been charged with kidnapping, and police say further charges are possible. The couple have not commented. Fourteen people have been taken to hospital for treatment, and 132 have been reunited with their families. One former patient told a local broadcaster that chaining was common practice, though he said the centre had helped him overcome addiction. The couple reportedly charged 3,000 rand a month per person, with almost half going to the church.

The case reflects a wider problem. Illegal rehabilitation centres have spread in South Africa as drug use has risen, and the social development department said last year it had found more than 100 unlawful facilities, mostly in Gauteng. The couple are expected to appear in a local court on Monday. The story has no direct market relevance.

stories.story:
Faber, the publisher of Irish novelist Sally Rooney, has stopped supplying her books in the UK. In a statement, the publisher said current UK legislation meant it could not pass UK earnings on to Rooney for her work, and it described that as an unconscionable position for a publisher. It said it had acted in full agreement with the author.

The decision follows Rooney's announcement last year that she would donate proceeds from her books to Palestine Action. The UK government banned that group in July last year under terrorism legislation, saying it had caused serious damage to property and was involved in terrorism. It was the first time a terrorist designation had been applied to a group that does not call for violence against people. Rooney has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and she has said she would continue supporting the group, while saying she has stopped attending UK events out of fear of arrest.

The ban has drawn criticism. UN human rights chief Volker Türk urged the UK to reverse it, calling it disproportionate, and Amnesty International UK said the definition of terrorism was too broad. Several thousand people have been arrested in the UK for supporting the group, mostly for carrying placards or wearing T-shirts. The High Court ruled against the ban in February, but the Court of Appeal later overturned that ruling, and the case is due before the Supreme Court next month. The United States also sanctioned the group in August.

Rooney has said she is prepared to accept the consequences. For readers, the story is mainly about freedom of expression, publishing and the legal status of the ban, rather than a commercial change for the author's market. The state has recorded 225 hospitalisations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths, and officials are investigating a sixth reported death. Children and teenagers aged five to 19 make up 42 percent of cases, while adults aged 20 and over account for 41 percent.

In response, the CDC is sending a disease detective from its Epidemic Intelligence Service to work with state health officials. The deployment follows a request from Pennsylvania for federal assistance. The state has expanded vaccination efforts, with more than 5,900 MMR doses given at 202 pop-up clinics since late April. New York's governor declared a statewide disaster emergency on 5 October, which runs until 4 November. The order widens the range of healthcare professionals who can give vaccines and gives nurses more flexibility to order testing.

The outbreak comes against a longer-term decline in childhood vaccination. CDC data show kindergarten measles vaccination coverage fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. The agency estimates that about 280,000 kindergarteners are at risk because of gaps in coverage. stories.story:
The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into a dispute over the founding of Your Party, a leftwing party that split as it was set up last year. Police said they opened the inquiry after receiving a report in September 2025 about alleged unauthorised access to a political party's database. A man was arrested on suspicion of an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990. He was released pending further inquiries and has not been charged. A woman in her 30s was interviewed under caution earlier in the investigation, and she has also not been charged.

The party was founded in summer 2025 by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana, who both now sit as Your Party MPs. Tensions grew after Sultana launched a membership portal that Corbyn called a false membership system. The Information Commissioner's Office had earlier advised that, although it was taking no further action on the portal, it may have involved serious criminal activity and should be referred to police. Police have not said which party the inquiry concerns, and sources told the Guardian it is linked to the long-running dispute over the party's founding.

Your Party said it would not comment further on the police investigation and that its systems were secure and the incident was isolated. The party has struggled to make a national impact, while the Green Party has seen its membership rise sharply. stories.headline: Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women
stories.claim: A 28-year-old Iranian woman was killed by her brother and husband in an alleged honour killing, sparking outrage and debate on violence against women.
stories.summary: Maryam Yarmohammadi, a 28-year-old mother of two, was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island on 5 October and died in hospital. Both men were arrested. DW examines the case as an example of so-called honour killings in Iran and the legal and social factors that allow them. It cites a 2020 Police Academy study and a UN report of at least 179 femicides in 2024. The case has provoked grief and outrage online, alongside victim-blaming comments.
key_points: Maryam Yarmohammadi was killed on 5 October on Qeshm Island by her brother and husband, both of whom have been arrested.
Around 50 relatives reportedly gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests, saying death was the least severe punishment.
A 2020 Iranian Police Academy study said honour killings accounted for up to 45% of murders in some conservative provinces.
A UN Special Rapporteur reported at least 179 women were killed by family members in 2024.
Iranian law allows victims' relatives to demand retribution or pardon, which creates a conflict of interest where the perpetrator is a relative.
stories.story:
Maryam Yarmohammadi, a 28-year-old mother of two, was attacked with knives in the early hours of 5 October on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her brother and husband were named as the attackers, and she died shortly afterwards in hospital. Both men have been arrested. Media reports say about 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests, reportedly believing death was the least severe punishment she deserved. What she was accused of has not been publicly reported.

DW places the case within a recognised pattern of honour killings, in which men are expected to erase a perceived dishonour to the family. Conduct regarded as dishonourable can be defined by family and social norms and may include something as ordinary as talking to an unrelated man. Women accused in this way often have little chance to defend themselves. Women's rights groups, including the Campaign to End Honor Killings, say they have sometimes been able to relocate threatened women, but there appeared to be no local group able to help her in this region.

The article also sets out legal concerns. Iranian law applies retribution in some offences including murder, and victims' relatives can either demand the death penalty or pardon the killer. Where the alleged killer is among those relatives, a serious conflict of interest arises. A 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy said honour killings accounted for up to 45% of murders in some conservative western and southern provinces, and a UN Special Rapporteur reported at least 179 family-related femicides in 2024.

The killing prompted wide grief and anger on social media, although many comments blamed the victim. Commentators quoted in the piece argue that cultural, legal and economic factors reinforce violence against women. The article also notes progress over decades, such as women's right to drive and vote, and the influence of the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' movement. The case is likely to keep attention on whether Iran's legal system will protect women from family violence.

sources.title: Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women

stories.summary: Thousands of protesters gathered in Connaught Place in New Delhi, waving national flags and demanding the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar. The rally was called by the youth 'Cockroach' movement, whose founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained beforehand. Critics say a voter list review has removed over 130 million names since last year and disproportionately affects Muslims. The Election Commission and the government deny the allegations.

Movement founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police before the protest.
An ongoing voter list review has reportedly removed more than 130 million names since last year.
Critics say the review is politically motivated and disproportionately affects minorities, particularly Muslims.
The Election Commission and Modi's government deny the allegations, saying the revision removes duplicate and ineligible entries.
stories.story:
Thousands of people rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, on Friday 16 October. Protesters waved the Indian flag and demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the country's election chief. The demonstration was called by the youth 'Cockroach' movement, and its founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the event. Central Park was closed on Friday and Saturday in anticipation of the protests.

The protests are fuelled by an ongoing review of voter lists, which critics say has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Opponents argue the exercise is politically motivated, could disenfranchise millions more and has had a disproportionate effect on minorities, particularly Muslims. The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration reject these claims and say the review aims to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

The rally follows a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi a week earlier. Police had initially asked people not to join the rally and offered a small, permitted gathering instead. Modi has not commented publicly, while some party leaders described the demonstrators as 'anarchists' and suggested, without evidence, that they had foreign backing.

The Cockroach movement began online this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites, and it has since grown into a nationwide youth protest movement. It forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for a leader who has been in power for more than 12 years. It is unclear whether the protests will develop into a broader political movement, as Modi's government remains electorally strong and anger over voter lists may not directly benefit the opposition.

stories.story:
Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust has said that two members of its staff may have accessed, or attempted to access, medical and incident information about William Chapman without a legitimate reason. Chapman, 24, was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on the previous Saturday. The trust says the concern was identified through its own proactive audits, and it has begun an investigation into the circumstances and the actions of the individuals involved.

The trust has also reported the matter to the Information Commissioner's Office, the UK data protection regulator, and says Chapman's family already knows of the potential breach. It has offered its condolences to the family and said it will keep them informed as the inquiry continues. It stressed that it takes patient confidentiality seriously and has systems in place to protect information.

At an inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court, heard on Thursday, it was said that Chapman had died of multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction. He had climbed over two fences and entered the tiger enclosure at about 13:30 on the Saturday. Park staff secured the animal and paramedics confirmed his death at the scene. Senior coroner Nicola Mundy noted that he had a history of mental illness, including a diagnosis of schizophrenia, but was described as highly functioning and independent with no care requirements.

The case is distressing for the family and raises questions about how NHS staff handle sensitive records in high-profile incidents. The investigation's findings and any action taken against the staff involved are yet to be announced.

stories.headline: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial
stories.claim: The Chancellor is reportedly considering a bank tax rise, including restoring the surcharge from 3% to 8%, in the October budget.
stories.summary: A Guardian editorial argues the government should tax UK banks more heavily, citing large banking profits driven by higher interest rates. It says the chancellor is reportedly considering restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise about £2bn a year. The piece cites several proposals, including a windfall tax, and argues banks cannot be too big to fail and too big to tax.
key_points: The Guardian argues Britain's largest banks have earned windfall profits from higher interest rates.
The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, worth around £2bn a year.
The Big Four banks reportedly made £29bn in the first half of 2026, up a fifth on 2025.
Other proposals cited include a 2.5% levy on interest-free deposits and a windfall tax on net income.
stories.story:
In an editorial, The Guardian argues that Britain should tax its banks more heavily. The piece says the sector's profits have risen sharply because of higher interest rates rather than better products. It cites a campaign group's estimate that the four biggest UK banks made £29bn in the first half of 2026, up about a fifth on the previous year. The editorial also says the Bank of England pays banks interest on their reserves, with the Treasury effectively covering the cost.

The editorial reports that the chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year. It argues this would recover only a modest share of the sector's gains. It points to other options, including a 2.5% levy on interest-free deposits, which a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests could raise more than £11bn, and a windfall tax on profits above a threshold, which the campaign group says could raise £19bn from the UK arms of the big four banks. The paper also cites Margaret Thatcher's 1981 windfall tax on banks as a precedent.

The banks argue that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that lending would fall and that profits will not last. The editorial rejects this, noting that banks spent £7.7bn on dividends and buybacks in early 2026 without, according to the Bank of England, affecting lending. It also highlights that banks are paying their highest bonuses since 2008.

The Guardian's proposals are opinion and reflect calls for tax reform rather than a government decision. Any change would depend on the chancellor's October budget, and bank shares could react if a tax rise is confirmed.
stories.likelihood_reason: Based on a Guardian report of government considerations, not an official announcement; the budget is set for 28 October.

stories.headline: Women see five or six doctors to figure out menopause symptoms. A top Novartis exec says AI could finally connect the dots
stories.claim: A Novartis executive says AI could help connect fragmented care for menopause and other women's health conditions.
stories.summary: At a Fortune summit, Novartis US executive Reshema Kemps-Polanco argued that AI could help link up the many specialists women see for symptoms such as menopause. Paula Schneider of the Institute Advancing Women's Health said women typically see five or six doctors, and that medical training covers midlife health only briefly. Both speakers stressed the need for human clinicians to remain involved. The comments were made as views, not as a company announcement.
key_points: Women reportedly see five or six doctors on average to manage menopause symptoms.
Schneider said future OB-GYNs get only about two hours of training on midlife health.
Novartis's Kemps-Polanco said AI could connect records and help diagnose conditions sooner.
Novartis is working on autoimmune conditions, where Sjögren's disease diagnosis can take about four years.
GoodRx's CEO said care should involve a real clinician rather than being fully AI-enabled.
stories.story:
At the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, speakers discussed how women with menopause symptoms often struggle to get joined-up care. Paula Schneider, chief executive of the Institute Advancing Women's Health, said women on average see five or six doctors while trying to piece together their symptoms, which can include sleep problems, joint stiffness and hot flashes. She said there is little holistic care available and that medical training gives future obstetrician-gynaecologists only a very small amount of teaching on midlife health.

Reshema Kemps-Polanco, an executive vice president at Novartis US, argued that AI could help connect these separate parts of care sooner. She said patients often see a dermatologist, a rheumatologist and a primary care doctor, and their records are not always linked. She described her own experience of typing symptoms into an AI tool while in an emergency room, saying it helped her prepare for a conversation with doctors although she was unsure how accurate it was. Novartis is working on autoimmune conditions, and she said patients with Sjögren's disease wait an average of four years for a diagnosis.

The panel was sponsored by Novartis. Wendy Barnes, chief executive of GoodRx, cautioned that women should still expect a human clinician to be involved, and that care should be backed by clinical evidence rather than being fully driven by AI. Schneider's institute is also working with a certification company to build AI-assisted training for clinicians. The remarks are opinions from a sponsored discussion rather than announced policy or new data, so the proposed benefits remain untested.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; Novartis is mentioned only as a sponsor and speaker.

stories.headline: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis

stories.summary: Uber and Wayve's limited robotaxi service in London, which started in September with safety drivers on board, faces mounting opposition. The London Assembly transport committee has called for Transport for London to have full power to permit or suspend operations. stories.story:
Opposition is growing to the rollout of robotaxis in London, with drivers, politicians and the city's transport authority all raising concerns. Uber and Wayve started limited autonomous taxi services in the capital in September, and more than 100,000 people are reported to be on Uber's waitlist. These services still have a human safety driver in the front seat, and driverless trials have expanded to Manchester this week.

The London Assembly's transport committee has published a critical report, arguing there is considerable uncertainty about the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles. Its concerns include the effect on public transport and congestion, and safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. The committee wants Transport for London to have full power to permit or suspend operations. Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can run, so for fully driverless services TfL could only grant or refuse consent. TfL reportedly sees parallels with Uber's early years in London, when it was twice refused licence renewal as not fit and proper.

Uber drivers are protesting. The App Drivers and Couriers Union plans demonstrations outside Wayve's London base this Saturday, following a similar protest at Waymo's Park Royal base in August. Drivers interviewed described falling earnings and fears that they could lose their livelihoods, and one said the robotaxis could leave older drivers struggling to adapt. A recent thinktank report cited in the piece estimates that more than 400,000 UK drivers, including 121,000 in London, could be affected.

The companies see London as a valuable market, given its size as a private hire market and its role as a European base. Uber has also said it plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide from next year. The coming months will show whether City Hall and the government move to give TfL more control, and how the protests and regulation shape the rollout.
stories.market_take: Potential regulatory limits on robotaxis could affect Uber's autonomous plans, though the near-term financial effect looks modest.

stories.headline: Fake calendar invites hit thousands of businesses in Microsoft credential phishing campaign
stories.claim: Check Point reports large phishing campaigns using fake calendar invites to steal Microsoft 365 login credentials.
stories.summary: Security firm Check Point Research has warned of several large-scale phishing campaigns that abuse calendar invites to harvest Microsoft 365 and other login credentials. The lures arrive either as .ics attachments that slip past email filters or as links that redirect victims to fake sign-in or payment pages. Check Point says the volume is rising fast, with more than 740,000 emails in the first two weeks of October. The findings highlight how routine business features can be turned into an effective attack route.
key_points: Attackers send fake calendar invites as .ics attachments or links to harvest login credentials.
Attachment-based invites often pass email filters because the file type is harmless on its own.
Event descriptions, locations or QR codes can direct victims to spoofed Microsoft 365 sign-in or payment pages.
Check Point counted over 302,000 flagged phishing emails sent to more than 40,000 organisations.
Daily volume reportedly rose from a few thousand a month in April to over 740,000 in early October.
stories.story:
Check Point Research has raised the alarm about several large-scale phishing campaigns that exploit the everyday habit of sharing calendar invitations in business. The attackers aim to steal Microsoft 365 and other login details. The researchers identified two main approaches. In the first, invites are sent as .ics attachments, which tend to pass email filters because the file type itself is harmless. When a recipient opens or accepts the invite, the entry lands in their calendar, sometimes automatically, and the description, location or an embedded QR code can point to a fake sign-in page or a fraudulent payment portal. In the second, the email contains a link that redirects the victim away from their calendar. This is easier to set up but more likely to be caught by security filters, though a fake Microsoft Teams invite example showed a join link leading to a third-party credential-harvesting page.

The scale is significant. Check Point said its new detection layer had flagged more than 302,386 unique phishing emails sent to over 40,000 organisations. The campaigns averaged more than 8,300 emails per active day, came from more than 33,000 sender domains and over 247,000 sender addresses, and the researchers say activity is accelerating. The busiest day so far was 8 October, with almost 200,000 emails. The firm dates a sharp surge to 25 September 2026.

Phishing remains one of the most common and cost-effective ways to compromise organisations. The article notes that the attacks themselves involve no software vulnerability or malware, which is why they are hard to block with technical controls alone. Defence therefore relies heavily on staff awareness, including treating unsolicited invites and urgent requests to log in or download files with suspicion. The report suggests the campaigns are continuing to grow, so security teams and employees may need to watch calendar-based lures closely.
stories.market_take: Mostly a security awareness story; it may modestly support demand for email security vendors.

stories.story:
A new online tool called CiteProof has been launched to help lawyers catch fabricated case law in court documents. The service is designed to crawl briefs and filings for citations that do not exist or quotations that are misstated before they reach a court, where errors can lead to sanctions, fines or public rebuke from judges.

The company says its approach is deliberately free of artificial intelligence. Rather than using language models or probabilistic methods, it runs deterministic searches of public court records to see whether cited material exists. According to the company, the only data leaving its servers is text strings taken from citations, which are checked against CourtListener. It says everything runs in the United States and nothing is sent to an LLM. The firm admitted that some vibe-coding was used to build the platform.

The article sets out the background of AI hallucinations in legal work. It cites a Georgia court decision that was vacated after an order was found to contain fictional citations, and an Anthropic case in which citations in a declaration were wrong and the lawyers blamed Claude. CiteProof does not assess the strength of arguments, only whether the citations are real.

Pricing starts with limited free individual checks for citations or statutes. Paid users can access in-depth reports, quotation checking and bulk scanning. A single brief costs $49, a five-pack costs $199, and law firms can pay $499 a month for 200 brief reviews. Whether the product gains traction will depend on how many firms see it as worth the cost compared with manual checking.

stories.story:

One example is an account called Aylen Skye, which has around 250,000 followers and posted a near-verbatim version of a joke by the comic Julia Jasunas. Jasunas says she reported the video to Meta for impersonation, but was told it did not breach the guidelines because the account was not pretending to be her.

WIRED says it identified eight comics whose videos have been replicated by similar AI-generated accounts, many of which follow one another. The copies are often polished, with better lighting, sound and tighter outfits, and some are reported to attract more engagement than the originals. The accounts also post AI-generated interviews with television hosts and occasionally offensive jokes. Another account, Tiffany Sloane, which has more than 375,000 Instagram followers and links to an OnlyFans profile, was described by comic George Brett Olson as having copied his joke, and he says Meta also found no breach.

The piece explains that Instagram's rules prohibit impersonation but do not generally cover copying content that is not copyrighted. The platform also allows AI content provided it is labelled, and labelling is inconsistent across these accounts. Skye did not respond to WIRED's request for comment. Comics have complained about similar accounts since June, and the technology behind the clones has improved rapidly.

The comics quoted want clearer rules to protect creators before the problem grows. Meta has not, in the material provided, offered a wider policy response. stories.summary: This edition of Ars Technica's Rocket Report covers several launch industry developments. Reflect Orbital bought two launches from India's Skyroot Aerospace, LEAP is targeting a 2028 debut for its Bighorn rocket, and Rocket Lab has delayed Neutron to 2027. Stoke Space has shipped its Nova upper stage for testing, and a Falcon 9 launched US military data relay satellites. The items point to growing demand for launch capacity.
key_points: Reflect Orbital bought two launches from Skyroot Aerospace, one on Vikram-1 and one on Vikram-1U.
Vikram-1 became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit in July.
LEAP plans to begin dedicated small-satellite launches in 2028 with its Bighorn rocket.
Rocket Lab said Neutron will not fly until 2027 because of a defect in carbon composite tank structures.
Stoke Space has shipped its reusable Nova upper stage for cryo-proof and hotfire testing.
A Falcon 9 launched the fourth plane of SDA Tranche 1 Transport Layer satellites.
stories.story:
The latest Rocket Report highlights several developments across the launch industry. California-based Reflect Orbital, which plans to use in-space mirrors to deliver sunlight on demand, has bought two launches from Indian firm Skyroot Aerospace. One will use the Vikram-1 rocket, which reached orbit in July as the first privately developed Indian rocket to do so, and the other will fly on an upgraded version, Vikram-1U. Reflect plans to launch its first satellite on a Falcon 9 rideshare next year.

Colorado-based LEAP is preparing to enter the dedicated small-satellite launch market, with a first orbital attempt planned for 2028. Its Bighorn rocket is designed to carry about 145 kilograms to low Earth orbit and is being built at a new factory near Denver, initially producing six vehicles a year. Rocket Lab, meanwhile, said its Neutron rocket will not fly until 2027, after a problem with small voids in the carbon-fibre forward dome of the first-stage tank. The delay was widely expected within the industry.

Elsewhere, Stoke Space has moved the reusable upper stage of its Nova rocket to its Moses Lake test site for cryogenic proof and hotfire tests, a step towards a launch next year. A Falcon 9 also launched the fourth plane of the US Space Development Agency's Tranche 1 data relay satellites from Vandenberg. The report notes concern that US launch capacity could tighten as SpaceX moves from Falcon 9 towards Starship.
stories.market_take: Rocket Lab's Neutron delay may weigh modestly on investor sentiment towards the company.

stocks.reason: Neutron delay to 2027 pushes back a key future revenue source.

stories.headline: SK hynix’s U.S. Subsidiary Has An Ace Up Its Sleeve To Soften China-Related Restrictions; Hiring Lobbying Veteran Who Has Been A 30-Year Acquaintance Of Donald Trump
stories.claim: SK hynix's US subsidiary Solidigm reportedly hired Ballard Partners and plans a Nasdaq listing and a US plant.
stories.summary: Reports by Chosun, relayed by Wccftech, say SK hynix's US subsidiary Solidigm hired lobbying firm Ballard Partners in September. The move is said to aim at easing China-related export restrictions, with a possible Nasdaq listing as early as 2027 and a US plant. The Democratic Party of Korea has reportedly objected to the listing plan. None of these plans has been confirmed by the companies.

A US manufacturing site is seen as a way to win favour with US trade policymakers.
stories.story:
Chosun has reported that SK hynix's US subsidiary, Solidigm, signed a contract with the lobbying firm Ballard Partners on 24 September. Ballard is run by Brian Ballard, who is described as having a long relationship with Donald Trump and a reputation as one of the country's most effective lobbyists. The firm reportedly has a team that includes former Trump administration officials. Wccftech, which relays the report, says the aim is to help Solidigm navigate US trade rules.

The report says Solidigm is preparing for a Nasdaq listing as early as 2027, a plan that has drawn concern in South Korea over dual-listing issues because SK hynix's main operations are at home. The Democratic Party of Korea has reportedly voiced opposition. Separately, the company is said to want approval to ship US equipment to China, where a NAND flash production facility is being built, and the proceeds of a listing and shipments could fund a US manufacturing plant.

The context is US restrictions on chip technology exports to China, which have made trade harder for major chipmakers. NAND flash prices have reportedly risen by as much as 700 percent since mid-2023, making production expansion more attractive. The article is a secondary report with no official comment from SK hynix or Solidigm, and it does not say whether the lobbying will succeed. Any Nasdaq listing would still need regulatory and board approvals.

stories.story:
Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, has seen its online delivery dates pushed back sharply after preorders opened. The Verge reports that within less than an hour of preorders going live at 8AM ET on Friday, Apple's website showed late January delivery for every configuration. The device is due to reach stores on 23 October, and Apple usually holds some units back for in-store sales, so customers may be able to buy one sooner in person.

Apple announced the Duo in September. It uses a shorter, passport-style folding design similar to one Samsung introduced earlier in the year. The starting price is $1,999 for the 256GB model, which is offered in two finishes, star white and night sky. Preorders remain open, although buyers face a long wait.

The long delivery window could reflect strong demand for a first foldable from Apple, limited supply, or a combination of both. Apple has not explained the situation publicly in the report. The next signal will be how quickly stock improves after the on-sale date and whether the wait times shorten, which would indicate how much supply Apple can produce.

The move reflects a wider trend in which platforms place summarised answers at the top of search results. For creators and publishers, that may mean less traffic. Whether the feature changes viewing habits in practice is something to watch in the coming months.

stories.summary: According to The Information, developers including PayPal and Epic Games have raised concerns with the US Department of Justice about a possible settlement of its antitrust case against Apple. The DOJ reportedly favours a negotiated resolution and has asked for ideas on improving iPhone interoperability. Critics doubt the changes would go far enough. key_points: Developers including PayPal and Epic Games have raised concerns with the DOJ.

stories.story:
According to a report by The Information, developers are questioning whether a settlement of the US government's antitrust case against Apple would meaningfully loosen the company's control over the iPhone. PayPal and Epic Games are named among companies that have raised concerns with the Department of Justice. Officials reportedly favour a negotiated resolution and have asked developers for suggestions on improving how the iPhone works with other firms' products.

The discussions centre on interoperability, including access for rival accessories and payment services. Critics argue that rival smartwatches lack much of the integration Apple Watch enjoys, and that competing payment apps still face disadvantages even though they now have access to NFC for contactless payments. The DOJ filed its lawsuit in March 2024, alleging that restrictions on messaging, digital wallets, smartwatches, cloud gaming and multipurpose apps protected Apple's smartphone monopoly. Apple rejected those claims and argued that the proposed remedies would undermine its ability to design integrated products.

Some issues have moved on since the case began. Apple added RCS support to Messages with iOS 18, which improves messaging with Android phones, and it expanded NFC access for third-party contactless payments from iOS 18.1. The Information reports that Apple had earlier offered some interoperability concessions to avert the lawsuit. The report suggests Apple could still resist the broader changes developers want, which would leave talks without agreement. One company quoted doubted Apple would accept terms developers would consider satisfactory.

The report does not describe a settlement as agreed. Any deal would still need to be reached and approved, and its scope remains open.
stories.market_take: A settlement that forces broader iPhone openness could modestly weigh on Apple's services revenue, though the outcome is far from settled.

stories.headline: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost
stories.claim: A Center for AI Safety dashboard tracks AI-attributed job cuts and estimated wage losses by US state.
stories.summary: The Center for AI Safety has published a Wage Loss Dashboard that maps job cuts companies have linked to AI since January 2026 and estimates the annual wage losses they represent. Nationally it counts just over 117,000 AI-attributed cuts, worth an estimated $8.5 billion in yearly wages, or about $25 per person. California shows the highest concentration, with over 27,000 cuts and about $56 per person. The dashboard uses Challenger, Gray and Christmas layoff reports and Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data. Its creators stress that state figures are estimates rather than observed AI layoffs, and that the tool excludes job creation and productivity effects.
key_points: The dashboard counts just over 117,000 job cuts attributed to AI in the US so far in 2026, with an estimated $8.5 billion in annual wage losses.
On a per-person basis the national figure is about $25 a year, ranging from $56 in California to $14 in Alaska.
State figures are modelled by applying the national share of AI-cited cuts to each state's announced layoffs, not counted directly.
The data come from Challenger, Gray and Christmas layoff reports and Bureau of Labor Statistics and Census figures.
In 2025, Challenger reports recorded over 54,000 job cuts companies publicly linked to AI, about one in 20 layoffs.
The dashboard excludes AI-created jobs, productivity gains and re-employment, so it gives a partial picture.
stories.story:
The Center for AI Safety, a research organisation, has launched a Wage Loss Dashboard that tries to show how job cuts linked to artificial intelligence affect household incomes in the United States. The tool maps layoffs announced since January 2026, including September data added this month, and lets users view national or state totals. Nationally it records just over 117,000 cuts that companies have attributed to AI this year, which it estimates equates to around $8.5 billion in lost annual wages.

The dashboard converts job cuts into wage losses by multiplying them by average salaries, then divides the result by state population to show a per-person figure. Across the country that comes to about $25 a year. California has the largest concentration of cuts, with more than 27,000, and a figure of $56 per person. Alaska records only 138 cuts, or $14 per person. The creators are clear that state numbers are estimates produced by applying the national share of AI-cited cuts to each state's announced job losses, rather than observed AI layoffs.

The project comes amid growing public concern about AI and employment after several years of steady corporate layoffs. Challenger, Gray and Christmas identified more than 54,000 job cuts linked to AI in 2025, roughly one in twenty layoffs that year. The researchers argue that the ripple effects of lost income reach local shops, small businesses and rents, and that states with large tech and media sectors are more exposed.

The dashboard has clear limits. It does not count jobs created by AI, productivity gains or re-employment, and experts do not agree on how much AI will stimulate the economy compared with displacing workers. There is also no single definition of an AI-linked layoff, and companies do not always disclose their reasons fully. A separate tracker, Jobloss.ai, run by the Alliance for Secure AI, uses a stricter test of at least 100 jobs cut at once with an explicit AI reference. The same dashboard also tracks how well AI agents complete remote freelance tasks, using the Remote Labor Index, where the best agent's success rate has risen sharply since launch.

stories.headline: The ultra-rich are spending one million dollars a day fighting California’s proposed billionaire tax
stories.claim: Tech billionaires have raised over $340m to fight California's Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% wealth tax, which is set for a November vote.
stories.summary: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to oppose Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on California's billionaires, according to state filings. The campaign against it reportedly spends over $1m a day. The measure goes to voters in early November and polling shows a narrowing lead for the yes side. Two rival measures, Props 41 and 42, could block the tax even if it passes.
key_points: Opponents of Prop 40 have raised more than $340m, and spend over $1m a day, according to state disclosures.
Prop 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California's billionaires, mostly funding healthcare.
Sergey Brin has reportedly given at least $102m, and Eric Schmidt more than $42m, to the no campaign.
A late-September University of California poll had 45% yes and 42% no, down from a 7-point lead a month earlier.
Props 41 and 42 could stop the tax from taking effect if they receive more yes votes than Prop 40.
stories.story:
The Guardian reports that tech billionaires have poured more than $340m into a campaign against Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on California's billionaires. According to state financial disclosures, the opposition campaign is spending more than $1m a day. The proceeds of the tax would mostly go to healthcare programmes, with some money for education and food assistance. Voters will decide the measure in early November.

The campaign has split Democrats. Supporters include the state's major unions, Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna. Opponents include both the Democratic and Republican gubernatorial candidates and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Major donors to the no campaign include Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt, Tony Xu, Patrick Collison and Chris Larsen, with Google co-founder Sergey Brin the largest contributor at a reported $102m. The yes campaign has raised just under $33m, mostly from a healthcare union.

Polling has shifted. A late-September University of California survey showed 45% of likely voters backing the tax and 42% opposed, a much smaller lead than the 7-point advantage seen a month earlier. Two countermeasures, Props 41 and 42, were placed on the ballot by opponents. If either gets more yes votes than Prop 40, it would block the billionaire tax even if Prop 40 passes. A political science professor quoted in the article said voter confusion tends to favour no votes.

The debate is being watched as a possible first step toward wealth taxes in other states, since California has more billionaires than any other state. Supporters frame the measure around affordability, a major midterm issue. The result could shape how other states approach taxing large fortunes, and the outcome remains uncertain given the tight polling and the heavy spending on both sides.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect, though the outcome could influence sentiment around wealth taxes for high-net-worth founders and investors.

stories.story:
Representative Ritchie Torres of New York's 15th congressional district has introduced the Power To The Players Act. The proposed law would direct the Federal Trade Commission to create regulations on video game ownership, with the aim of curbing practices that consumer advocates see as unfair. Under the bill, buying a game would give the buyer ownership of it rather than a licence to play it. Games with online features would also have to provide an offline mode before the supporting servers are shut down.

The issue has grown among players, who complain that games can expire even though they cost more than before, and that in-game monetisation can be aggressive. A Pennsylvania state senator, John Kane, has also introduced a state bill, the Protect Our Games Act, which would require publishers to offer an offline mode, community servers or a minimum refund of 25%.

The article points to recent examples that prompted the debate, including The Crew, which Ubisoft shut down in 2024 and which became unplayable. NBA 2K25 was also cited by Torres, with its online servers being shut down two years after release. The Stop Killing Games movement has pushed for offline modes, peer-to-peer patching and community servers, and it opposes the industry practice of selling licences rather than copies. The article notes that Sony's lawyers have argued in a class action that buyers would not reasonably expect a durable right to use a game.

The bill is at an early stage. Its exact definitions and details have not yet been released, and the article notes it is unclear whether a right to transfer digital purchases would be required. Passage is uncertain, and any final rules would depend on how the bill is drafted and how it fares in Congress.

stories.headline: Is AI interpretability close to a breakthrough? A new essay has researchers divided
stories.claim: A Goodfire researcher argues neural networks are far less tangled than assumed, but other researchers are divided on the claim.
stories.summary: Nick Cammarata of Goodfire has published an essay arguing that the inner workings of large AI models are much easier to understand than thought. He challenges the superposition explanation he helped shape. Reactions are divided: OpenAI's Roon calls it historic, while Google DeepMind's Neel Nanda urges caution. The results on language models are preliminary and not yet independently confirmed.
key_points: Cammarata argues that neurons in neural networks are far more interpretable than previously assumed.
He reinterprets the famous cat-car neuron as a V-shape detector.
He reports that about 90% of neurons in Qwen3-32B have one main job, with 2 to 4% unexplained.
OpenAI's Roon calls the work potentially historic, but says others must confirm it.
Google DeepMind's Neel Nanda says it does not change the broader picture.
stories.story:
Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the interpretability lab Goodfire, has published a long essay titled "Neural Networks Are Already Clean". He argues that the internal workings of large AI models are much easier to understand than researchers had assumed. In doing so he rejects the superposition explanation that he helped shape years earlier, which holds that networks pack unrelated concepts into the same neurons when they run short of space.

Cammarata now argues that some of the best-known examples were misread. He says the neuron once thought to respond to both cat faces and car fronts is in fact a V-shape detector. He also reinterprets a circuit from the earlier paper "Zoom In" as ordinary generalisation. For language models he offers preliminary figures: in Qwen3-32B, about 90% of neurons have one main job, around 7% have two related ones, and only 2 to 4% remain unexplained. Goodfire says it sees similar results in models with up to trillions of parameters, with AI agents doing much of the analysis.

Reactions are mixed. OpenAI employee Roon called the work potentially a major moment in scientific history, though he also noted that others still need to confirm the results and that interpretability advances could boost AI capabilities. Neel Nanda, who leads interpretability work at Google DeepMind, was more measured. He said the essay is interesting but does not fundamentally change the picture, and he doubts interpretability is close to being fully solved. His team has also deprioritised sparse autoencoders.

The stakes are significant for AI safety, since better tools to see what a model is doing could help detect deception or dangerous behaviour. For now, though, the claims rest on preliminary numbers and an essay rather than independent peer-reviewed replication, so the field is likely to test them further before drawing firm conclusions.

stories.summary: Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, opened for preorders on 16 October ahead of its 23 October release. It starts at $1,999 and costs up to $3,199 with 2TB of storage. stories.story:
Apple's first foldable iPhone, called the iPhone Duo, is now available to preorder ahead of its release on 23 October. Preorders opened at 8 a.m. ET on Friday 16 October. The device has a passport-style design, a nano-texture inner display, a hidden selfie camera, an A20 Pro chip and a graphite pipe inside its hinge to help with cooling. Apple announced the device in September after years of speculation.

Pricing starts at $1,999 for 256GB. A 512GB model costs $2,199 and a 1TB model costs $2,599. A 2TB version is priced at $3,199, which would make it the most expensive iPhone Apple has sold. Apple Store preorders sold out quickly and the device is on backorder there until January. Major US carriers showed delivery dates from November to December. Apple has reportedly raised production by 30 percent, based on a report from China's Securities Times, but this appears not to have been enough to meet demand.

Early hands-on reviews from several outlets are generally positive. Reviewers praised the feel of the hinge, the crease on the inner screen and the premium build. Criticisms include the matte finish of the inner display, the slippery edges, the placement of volume buttons and the absence of Face ID, which is replaced by Touch ID in the side button. Full reviews had not yet been published at the time of writing.

Carriers including AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon and Xfinity are offering trade-in and bill-credit deals that can reduce the effective price, usually when a trade-in or premium plan is included. Apple also offers trade-in credits and a leasing option through its Klarna-backed Upgrade programme. The launch is an important test for Apple's push into foldable phones, which the company has been slower to enter than some Android rivals.
stories.market_take: Strong early demand and supply limits could support Apple's hardware sales, while suppliers of hinges and displays may see gains.

stories.headline: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
stories.claim: Polymarket election markets saw over $600 million in trading largely from wash trading on losing long-shot candidates.
stories.summary: Two global election markets on Polymarket's offshore platform generated more than $600 million in trading volume, most of it on candidates who did not win. Analysis cited by WIRED and Ars Technica suggests much of the Ethiopian and Romanian market activity was wash trading, where accounts trade with each other to inflate volume. Polymarket says it flagged and blocked the accounts involved. Experts suggest traders may have been farming volume in hope of a future token.
key_points: Two Polymarket election markets generated over $600 million in volume, mostly on losing candidates.
In the Ethiopian market, about $284 million came from pairs of accounts trading with each other.
An analyst found over 98 percent of 38,000 trade loops produced no gain or loss, with a median hold time of nine seconds.
In the Romanian market, an analysis suggested 99.6 percent of volume in certain weeks was wash trading.
Polymarket says it flagged and blocked the accounts but did not explain why they could trade so much before action.
Experts suggest traders may have been farming activity in hope of a future Polymarket token.
stories.story:
Polymarket, the prediction market platform, has been linked to unusual trading patterns in two political markets, according to a report from Ars Technica that draws on WIRED's reporting. Two global election markets on its offshore platform together generated over $600 million in trading volume, far above what political markets usually attract. Most of the trading was on candidates who did not win.

In the Ethiopian market, the prime minister's party won a large majority in federal elections this summer. Yet about $41 million was traded on his chief of staff becoming the next leader, compared with $173,000 on the prime minister himself. Analysts say about $284 million of the total came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with one another. One researcher described it as volume manipulation. Polymarket said its team flagged the activity and blocked the accounts, though it did not say why they were able to trade so much before action was taken.

The Romanian market, which covered a 2024 election that was annulled over foreign interference fears, showed similar patterns. An algorithm used by researchers identified 99.6 percent of volume in certain weeks as likely wash trading. Researchers note that the identities of the traders are unknown, so the explanation cannot be fully proven. An analysis for WIRED suggested the most likely cause was activity farming, where users inflate volume in the hope of benefiting from a future Polymarket token. The company's marketing chief has said in the past that a token would come, without giving details.

The story highlights the risk that prediction market volumes can be distorted and used as a measure of public opinion. Wash trading is banned on regulated US exchanges and is prohibited by Polymarket's own terms. Prediction markets have grown rapidly, and questions about how they are monitored are likely to continue.
stories.market_take: Little direct market effect, though scrutiny of prediction markets could affect platforms and crypto-linked sentiment.

stories.claim: China has published draft rules requiring export licences for some large AI models, while Taiwan has made smuggling advanced chips to China a crime.
stories.summary: China has reportedly published draft export rules that could put 23 AI technologies, including large models and compute clusters, under a licensing regime. Open-weight models above 2 trillion parameters or trained on over 10^26 FLOPS would need approval, possibly affecting Moonshot AI's upcoming Kimi K3.1. Taiwan has separately moved to criminalise the export of advanced chips and servers to China. The rules are drafts and have not yet been implemented.

Open-weight models above 2 trillion parameters or trained on over 10^26 FLOPS would need Ministry of Commerce permission.

stories.story:
China has published draft rules that would bring 23 AI-related technologies under an export licensing regime, according to reports on social media and tech sites. The technologies include large models, AI agents and compute clusters. The most notable element is that Chinese AI labs may need explicit permission before releasing open-weight models with more than 2 trillion parameters, or models trained on more than 10^26 floating-point operations. The Ministry of Commerce is reportedly planning a streamlined and automatic licensing process.

The draft rules would apply to new open-weight models only, so existing models would not be affected. Moonshot AI is the company most likely to be affected because its Kimi K3.1 model is widely expected to launch soon and is reported to have more than 2 trillion parameters. Earlier leaked code suggested the model would include reasoning effort settings, a context window of 1 million tokens and an agent mode. Moonshot's predecessor, Kimi K3, drew attention earlier in the summer for a new attention architecture.

On the same day, Taiwan reportedly agreed, under its trade arrangement with the United States, to make the routing of advanced chips and servers to China a criminal offence. Taiwan already bans such exports, but until now prosecutors had to rely on other laws with a higher threshold for conviction. The timing of the two moves has drawn attention, though they are separate policies.

The Chinese draft has not yet been implemented, and the article notes that the rules may still change. Whether they will deter open release of Chinese models or merely add a bureaucratic step remains unclear. Investors in the chip and AI sectors may watch for any further detail on how the controls are applied.

stories.claim: Canonical has released Ubuntu 26.10 'Stonking Stingray' with a pre-release Linux 7.3 kernel and a new speech-to-text tool.
stories.summary: Ubuntu 26.10, codenamed Stonking Stingray, has been released on schedule, shipping with a Linux kernel 7.3 that is still at release candidate 7. The release includes Myna, a speech-to-text tool available as a technology preview, and updates across all flavours. The Register reviewer found it works well on supported hardware but is limited, with no understanding of punctuation or voice commands. Fedora 45 has been delayed by about a week.

stories.story:
Canonical has released Ubuntu 26.10, codenamed Stonking Stingray, on schedule. The release arrived about two weeks after the beta. The Register notes that it ships with Linux kernel 7.3 even though that kernel is still at release candidate 7, so machines will be updated to the final version once it is available. This reflects the faster kernel release cycle the Linux project adopted in 2024.

A headline feature is Myna, a speech-to-text system now available as a technology preview. In the reviewer's tests, it worked well with a USB headset but was poor with the laptop's built-in microphone. It revises text as the user speaks, but does not understand punctuation or spoken commands, which were typed out as words. The reviewer described it as impressive for a preview and useful for people with limited use of their arms, while noting that Windows and macOS have offered speech input for years.

The release also brings a Windows-style tiling pop-up in GNOME 51 and updated versions of all flavours, which has not happened for about a year. Changes include Budgie 10.10.3, Cinnamon 6.6.9, LXQt 2.4 and Lomiri apps in Ubuntu Unity. Core tools have been replaced with Rust versions, and the server edition includes ROCm 10.0 and OpenSSL 4. Canonical's disk encryption can not yet be upgraded from 26.04.

In related news, the Fedora 45 release has been delayed because no release candidate was ready, so it is expected about a week later than planned.

stories.headline: Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’
stories.claim: Sherry Turkle's new book argues chatbots should not use first-person language, warning of risks to human connection.
stories.summary: In an interview with Steven Levy in Wired, MIT professor Sherry Turkle discusses her new book, Artificial Intimacy, which warns that overreliance on chatbots threatens human connection. She argues that chatbots should not use the first person and criticises the phrase 'human in the loop' as a false comfort. Turkle says she has more hope now than six months ago that people will look at the intimate costs of AI. The piece is an opinion-led interview rather than a policy announcement.
key_points: Sherry Turkle's new book, Artificial Intimacy, is presented as a warning about overreliance on chatbots.
Turkle says her interviews during the pandemic changed her from neutral to alarmed.
She argues chatbots should not use the first person, though she does not call for a blanket ban.
She is sceptical of the 'human in the loop' idea, saying the human role is often limited to cleanup.
stories.story:
Wired has published an interview between Steven Levy and Sherry Turkle, the MIT professor and long-time researcher of how people interact with computers. Turkle's new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, is a more urgent work than her previous studies. She describes it as a warning that people's humanity is at risk from reliance on machines that act as tutors, friends and lovers.

Turkle says her change in tone came from interviews conducted during the pandemic, in which people told her they preferred to spend time with their chatbots. She argues that chatbots should not use the first person, saying they can be presented as companions in ways that feel intimate. She sees the risk as a slippery slope, where chatbots are used to replace therapy and where people treat them as the final step in practising conversation.

She is also critical of the term 'human in the loop', which she says often leaves people with little ability to change outcomes while giving a false sense of oversight. In her view, AI cannot replace human conversation because it has no experience of death, illness or love. She acknowledges that many people feel helped by chatbots, especially those who are lonely, but argues that loneliness reflects people abandoning one another.

Turkle says she has more hope than before that public debate will widen to include intimate uses of AI, alongside existing concerns about data centres and jobs. The interview gives a single expert's view and reflects an opinion position rather than a policy decision.

stories.headline: Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?
stories.claim: Azerbaijan's school headscarf restrictions have sparked rare child-led protests, arrests and criticism from Turkey.
stories.summary: DW reports on a rare wave of protests in Azerbaijan over a ban on headscarves in schools, which has drawn criticism from Turkey. Rules adopted in July, September and October tightened dress codes for pupils and teachers. Authorities detained 37 people, blocked Instagram and TikTok, and opened a criminal case. Amnesty International called for releases.
key_points: Schools have turned away girls wearing hijabs under a tightened uniform resolution, though the rule does not explicitly mention headscarves.
Protests, including children and some boys, have run for about a week, an unusual event in Azerbaijan.
On October 12 the Interior Ministry said 37 people were detained and a criminal case was opened, without identifying those held.
Turkey criticised the restrictions, and Azerbaijan's ruling party responded that close ties do not justify interference.
stories.story:
Azerbaijan is facing an unusual wave of protests over a dispute about Islamic headscarves in its schools. For nearly a week, children, including some boys showing solidarity, have demonstrated against the headscarf restrictions. Rallies are rare in the country, where police usually disperse public protests, and demonstrations involving children are described as unprecedented. Access to Instagram and TikTok was disrupted as videos spread, though the authorities have not explained the blocks.

The row stems from a series of legal changes. In July the education law was amended to reinforce secular education and require dress codes. In September a government resolution tightened school uniform rules and banned clothing that disrupts the uniform. The text does not mention the hijab, but some school administrators have applied it to headscarves. A further decision in October set dress rules for teachers, and reports say some women wearing headscarves have been prevented from teaching. The article notes that the constitution separates religion from the state.

On October 12 the Interior Ministry said 37 people had been detained over the protests, accusing them of confronting staff, damaging property and obstructing schools and traffic. A criminal case was opened. Activist Ilkin Huseynov was reportedly given 30 days' administrative detention after launching a project linking volunteer tutors with affected pupils. Officials and some observers link the rules to efforts to counter Iranian influence and religious groups, though the alleged foreign involvement has not been independently established. Amnesty International condemned the exclusion of girls and urged release of those detained for peaceful protest.

The controversy has also reached Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul on October 3, and an adviser to President Erdogan criticised the restrictions. Azerbaijan's ruling party said close relations do not justify interference in its internal affairs. For families, the immediate question is whether children can attend school without removing their headscarves.

stories.claim: Zelenskyy says Ukraine's military Starlink access is not fully restored, and seeks €70bn more from the EU for 2027.
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said the military's access to Starlink, specifically the Starshield military version, has not been fully restored after being throttled. Reuters reported the order came from inside the White House. Zelenskyy also asked the EU for an extra €70bn for 2027, with the European Commission agreeing a gap exists. The meeting took place amid a dispute with Donald Trump over Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and a failed energy ceasefire.

Reuters reports, citing US and Western officials, that the throttling order came from within the White House.

stories.story:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the Ukrainian military's access to Starlink has not yet been fully restored after a reduction in service speeds. He described the move as a dangerous and unpleasant surprise. Reuters reported that the order to slow the Starshield military version came from inside the White House, citing two US officials and a Western official. The Pentagon was reportedly informed. Ukraine uses the service to support air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones. Neither the intelligence withholding nor the throttling has been officially confirmed.

Zelenskyy met EU leaders in Brussels, where he asked for a further €70bn for 2027 to fund defence, weapons and resilience. He said the war would cost €155bn that year. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen agreed there was a gap of €70bn, though she expected other partners to cover part of it. The EU's current €90bn plan covers two-thirds of Ukraine's needs for 2026 and 2027, with the rest expected from partners such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.

The discussions came after US President Donald Trump criticised Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and said they were pushing up world oil prices. A proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. Von der Leyen said Russia had not respected it and the EU would propose a 22nd sanctions package while keeping existing sanctions in place until Russia stops the war. Zelenskyy also raised the idea of an EU-controlled custodian for Russia's €210bn of frozen assets, which Belgium opposes over the financial risk.

The dispute matters for defence contractors, satellite operators and energy markets. Oil and diesel supply, affected by both the Ukraine war and the wider conflict involving Iran, remain a concern for the global economy. The next steps include EU decisions on funding and sanctions, and clarity from Washington on the Starlink restrictions.
stories.market_take: Oil and diesel prices could move on refinery strikes and sanctions, and SpaceX-linked services face reputational and policy questions.

stories.headline: Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
stories.claim: Kenya has confirmed a third Bundibugyo Ebola case linked to its first patient, as questions arise over DRC aid funds.
stories.summary: Kenya's Health Ministry has confirmed a third case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients. The first Kenyan case, a man who died in Nairobi on 5 October, was linked to the epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kenya says 127 of 130 listed contacts have been traced and quarantined and that there is no community spread. Separately, the Africa CDC says more than $700m in donor money for DRC Ebola response is unaccounted for, which officials are disputing as premature to call embezzlement. A new province in DRC is also reportedly affected.

stories.story:
Kenya's Health Ministry has reported its third case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, ten days after confirming its first case and death in Nairobi. The latest patient is a 65-year-old woman described as a primary contact and close relative of the earlier cases. She has been in quarantine since 6 October and is receiving supportive care after testing positive.

The first Kenyan case involved a man who had been ill in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and later travelled by road to Uganda before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. He died on 5 October. The ministry says 127 of 130 listed contacts have been traced and quarantined, and it has stressed that the risk to the public remains low with no community spread.

The outbreak in the DRC is the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was detected in May. The Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine, and several candidate vaccines are in early human trials. Separately, the Africa CDC says aid groups report receiving $228m, with $127m spent and about $100m left, while donors disbursed about $962m to implementing organisations rather than the government. The agency said this left more than $700m unaccounted for, though its director said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.

Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba has told aid groups to disclose funding sources or risk being barred from working in the DRC and blacklisted across Africa. Two health officials also told Reuters that cases have been found in North Ubangi, the eighth affected province, though authorities have not yet officially announced this. The situation is a public health story with possible wider effects on aid transparency.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect, though the outbreak may affect healthcare and vaccine-related shares.

stories.story:
Alan Feeney, a Reform UK councillor, has resigned from Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council after undercover footage showed him making offensive remarks about Asian homeowners. The recordings were made for an ITV News investigation that ran over a year and was broadcast ahead of the May council elections. In the footage, Feeney describes an area as 'infested' with Asian families and calls them 'absolute parasites'. He is also heard saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.

Feeney has apologised, saying the comments were wrong and did not reflect his true beliefs. He has also left the party and been suspended from his job as a custodial manager with the prison service. The Ministry of Justice has called the remarks 'despicable' and says they will be investigated under its policy. Feeney had defected from the Conservatives to Reform last year and was elected to a Birmingham ward in May.

Two other Reform candidates filmed in Solihull, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, have also resigned. Samantha Gethen, the opposition leader on Solihull Council and a Reform member, said the resignations were the right thing to do and that by-elections will follow. Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he did not like what he heard, but argued the party acted quickly and that every party has 'bad apples'.

The affair adds to pressure on Reform over how it vets candidates, with Farage defending the party's procedures. The story is primarily political rather than economic and is unlikely to have any market impact, though it may affect the party's standing ahead of future elections.

stories.story:
Meta has updated the commercial terms that apply to businesses using its Meta Business Suite dashboard, and the change could allow the company to scrape a wide range of websites. According to a report by Nieman Lab, the wording gives Meta and its agents permission to crawl and copy any web pages linked to a business's products or services, and to use that content to develop and train its AI products. Legal experts cited by Nieman Lab reportedly agree that the terms cover this scraping.

The new rules take effect on 30 October. Meta is not offering an opt-out, which means publishers who want to keep their accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger or WhatsApp will effectively have to accept the crawling. The dashboard is used to manage those profiles and channels, so the reach of the terms extends well beyond a single platform.

The report suggests the move could help Meta avoid paying for licences to news content. High-quality, edited journalism is particularly valuable for training AI models, and several AI companies have already signed licensing agreements with publishers. Other publishers, including Ziff Davis, the parent company of ZDNET, have sued AI firms over training and over answers that reuse their content without attribution.

What happens next will depend on how publishers and regulators respond. Publishers could challenge the terms, seek clarification or move away from the platform, while the lawsuits already filed against AI firms may be used as a reference point. The story is based on the reported reading of the terms by legal experts rather than on a statement from Meta in this article.

stories.headline: Clashes grip Tirana as Albanian PM blames 'foreign hands' for mounting unrest
stories.claim: Protests in Tirana have entered a fourth day with clashes, and Prime Minister Rama blames unnamed foreign hands for the unrest.
stories.summary: Protests in Albania's capital Tirana turned violent for a fourth day on Friday, with clashes between demonstrators and police. Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed unnamed 'foreign hands' for the unrest, which he said aimed to hinder Albania's EU membership bid. Authorities reported 156 injured, including 97 police, and 160 detentions on Thursday. Protesters are demanding Rama's resignation over university conditions and tuition fees.

stories.story:
Protests in Albania's capital, Tirana, have turned violent for the fourth day running. Thousands of demonstrators have gathered since Tuesday to call for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, and to protest against conditions at universities and high tuition fees. On Friday, protesters clashed with police, who used tear gas and water cannon. Some demonstrators threw stones and burned rubbish bins to block roads, and protesters tried to force their way into government offices.

The unrest has caused damage across the city. Shopfronts were smashed, several government buildings were attacked, including the finance ministry, and masked groups were reported to be looting stores. Police said 160 people were detained for violence on Thursday. Interior Minister Ervin Demo said 156 people had been injured in recent days, including 97 police officers. He also said two police officers had been suspended after two instances of excessive force.

Rama blamed unnamed 'foreign hands' for fuelling the protests, saying they wanted to stop Albania joining the European Union. He did not provide details or evidence for the claim. He has repeatedly dismissed protesters' concerns in a similar way. Demonstrations have been going on for months, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of US President Donald Trump.

The sell-off in AI-related shares extended from chipmakers and data-centre suppliers into the debt that funds the sector. Bonds issued by CoreWeave, a neocloud provider that rents out computing capacity, fell to levels that signal financial distress.

Oil at $110 a barrel makes that inflation risk harder to dismiss, and could limit how quickly central banks are able to ease policy. Investors are now asking whether the huge spending on computing capacity will generate enough revenue to repay the debt raised to finance it.

The article does not describe official responses. The key questions for the coming weeks are whether the AI debt concerns spread further into credit markets and whether oil prices stay near current levels.

European leaders voiced support, but the Commission has been asked to propose financing and Belgium still opposes using frozen Russian assets.
