stories.story:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky turned to European allies in Brussels on Friday, asking for an additional €70 billion, roughly $79 billion, to fund the war against Russia next year. The request came amid a sharp deterioration in his relationship with US President Donald Trump, which followed the US easing sanctions on Moscow as part of a deal to supply diesel. Trump reportedly described Kyiv's actions as a disgrace after Zelensky ordered strikes on Russian refineries resumed.

Zelensky also asked for more Patriot missiles to counter Russian missile attacks. Disruption to a US-provided satellite communications system, Starshield from SpaceX, has reportedly hampered Ukraine's defence. SpaceX said it was not behind the disruption and a US official denied any Trump administration intervention. Zelensky said that speeds had not yet fully recovered but were being restored.

EU leaders expressed unity. European Council chief Antonio Costa called for more support and pressure, and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the situation as dire. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the figure had to be covered and asked partners to step in, and the Commission has been told to draft a financing proposal. Macron said the request would be analysed, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU would discuss it before the end of the year.

The EU is already paying instalments on a €90 billion loan for Kyiv that covers funding to the end of 2027, but Ukrainian authorities warn of a large budget gap. Calls to use around €200 billion of frozen Russian central bank assets have resurfaced, though there appears to be little momentum, as Belgium remains opposed. Whether the new funding is agreed will depend on negotiations that are still at an early stage.
stories.market_take: Ukraine funding and frozen Russian asset debates could affect European defence and sovereign bond sentiment modestly; the Trump-Zelensky rift is a wider political risk.

A grassroots protest movement against rising fuel prices is set to stage nationwide demonstrations in France on Saturday 17 October, with more than 1,000 events listed on a protest website. The actions include marches, roundabout blockades and gatherings outside petrol stations and oil depots. The movement started with a viral TikTok video from a young man frustrated by pump prices, and it has since been backed by left-wing politicians, including the Communist Party leader and the Green leader.

The protests also show solidarity with high-school students who have been demonstrating for almost a month to demand better classroom conditions. Those student protests have drawn scrutiny to police tactics. Police have opened internal investigations into 36 complaints of officer violence against protesters, including four children said to have been seriously hurt by explosive weapons and six with significant injuries. Other complaints involve blows, insults and alleged sexual assault.

The planned demonstrations draw comparisons with the 2018 Yellow Vest movement, which began over fuel prices and grew into a broader protest against economic inequality. Former figures from that movement are divided. Some say they did not coordinate the call, while others, including Jérôme Rodrigues, see the protests as a continuation of the student demonstrations. Activist Sophie Tissier, who registered earlier demonstrations with Paris police, has registered a protest on the Champs-Élysées for Saturday. Former figures also note that the current protests are more closely guided by political parties than the original movement was.

The article frames the protests as reflecting wider frustration over living standards, public services and political scandal. Organisers argue that the demands of the earlier movement have become more pressing. The coming weekend will show how large the turnout is and whether the police response to the student protests becomes a central issue.

stories.story:
A shooting at Silver Rail elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday ended after a bystander shot and killed the attacker. The family of the bystander, named in reports as Kaylub Giamanco, said in a statement on Friday that he fired the fatal shots. Authorities have not yet officially released his identity, though law enforcement has named the suspect as John J Griffin II, aged 16.

According to police, several children and a teacher were killed. Three children aged five, eight and 11, and a teacher died, while a seven-year-old child and another teacher were critically injured. Police chief Mike Krantz said officers arrived within minutes of multiple 911 calls and that a bystander had followed the suspect into the school and confronted him shortly before officers arrived. The suspect was armed with a pump-action shotgun that his mother had bought, according to the Associated Press.

The man is reported to have been driving home near the school when he heard gunshots. His family, which includes his brother Kameron, asked for privacy and said he does not want recognition, but wishes to thank first responders, school staff and the community. Combs was earlier placed in a special housing unit and lost 41 days of good-conduct credit, moving his release date to 2 March 2028. stories.story:
Sean 'Diddy' Combs, the music producer, has been moved from a federal prison in New Jersey to a low-security facility in Pennsylvania, according to the Associated Press and other outlets. The US Bureau of Prisons is transferring him from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, which lies south of Williamsport roughly 250 km west of New York City. The transfer was confirmed to AFP by a Bureau of Prisons spokesperson.

The move comes after weeks of reports about his conditions. In September, NBC News reported that he was enjoying aspects of his lifestyle at Fort Dix, including smuggled cognac, services from other inmates and a contraband phone. Separately, TMZ reported that he had been injured in a fight, but the Bureau of Prisons said that account was false. After the NBC report, Combs was placed in a special housing unit, and he lost 41 days of good-conduct credit, which pushed his release date back to 2 March 2028.

Combs was convicted on 2 July 2025 of prostitution-related charges involving transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters, and received a sentence of four years and two months. His spokesperson said the decision on placement rests with the Bureau of Prisons and hoped the new facility would allow him to focus on moving forward.

His lawyers are challenging the conviction and sentence, which they argue is too harsh. The Second Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in April and has not yet ruled. The story is mainly of interest to general news readers and has no direct market relevance.

stories.story:
Tesla has unveiled the second-generation Roadster, its long-delayed electric sports car, at an event in Texas on Thursday night. The angular, Cybertruck-influenced coupe looks very different from the concept shown in 2017, which had targeted a 1.9-second 0-60 time, 620 miles of range and a 2020 start of production. That deadline passed, and the car was delayed several times. The new version was presented as a showcase for Tesla, xAI and SpaceX, the companies led by Elon Musk.

The demonstration featured the car driving up a ramp onto a wall, held in place by underbody suction fans that Tesla says can generate up to 2 g of suction. It then performed a barrel roll in the air, using 10 SpaceX cold-gas thrusters, and later hopped over a row of Tesla vehicles. Musk said the car would be offered in three trim levels, including the Rocket Roadster, with production targeted for 2028.

Tesla's claimed performance figures include cornering above 2 g and a 0-60 mph time of one second, or 0.81 seconds with thrusters. These numbers have not been independently verified. The CNET writer is sceptical that the car shown was fully drivable, noting opaque windows and the implausibility of aerobatics for a battery-heavy EV, and suggests it was probably a remote-controlled test vehicle. The writer also doubts the flying Rocket version would be street-legal.

Tesla has not disclosed final prices or updated range estimates. Reservations are open at $50,000 on its Roadster page. The launch comes amid speculation about closer ties between Tesla and SpaceX, though the event itself did not confirm any merger.

stories.headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
stories.claim: US fiscal 2026 budget deficit reached $1.992 trillion, up 12% from the prior year.
stories.summary: The US Treasury reported a fiscal 2026 budget deficit of $1.992 trillion, about 12% above the prior year's $1.775 trillion. It is the third-largest annual deficit in US history, behind 2020 and 2021. Net interest topped $1 trillion, and corporate tax receipts fell by about $70 billion. Customs revenue was hit by refunds after a Supreme Court ruling.
key_points: The fiscal 2026 deficit was $1.992 trillion, up from $1.775 trillion in fiscal 2025.
It is the third-largest annual deficit after 2020 and 2021.
Net interest exceeded $1 trillion, compared with $970 billion the year before.
Corporate income tax receipts fell about $70 billion because of tax cuts passed last year.
Customs refunds following a Supreme Court ruling reduced net tariff revenue.
stories.story:
The US Treasury Department reported on Friday that the federal government ran a budget deficit of $1.992 trillion for fiscal 2026. That is about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit recorded in fiscal 2025. It is the third-largest annual deficit in US history, after only 2020 and 2021, when pandemic stimulus spending was at its peak. The year marks the 25th consecutive year in which the government ran a deficit, with the last surplus recorded in 2001.

The report shows several cost pressures. Social Security spending was close to $1.7 trillion, while Medicare cost almost $1.1 trillion. Net interest also topped $1 trillion, up from $970 billion in the previous year. Individual income tax receipts rose about 7% to more than $2.8 trillion, but corporate income tax receipts fell by roughly $70 billion, which the report links to tax cuts passed by Congress last year.

Customs duties hit a record gross level, but net customs revenue was reduced by refunds required after the Supreme Court ruled that many of the Trump administration's tariffs were unconstitutional. September alone recorded a deficit of $27 billion, compared with a surplus of $198 billion a year earlier. Bond traders have pushed the 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields to 24-year highs, and the total national debt has exceeded $40 trillion.
stories.market_take: A larger deficit and high yields may keep pressure on Treasury prices and interest-rate sensitive sectors.

stories.claim: Downing Street has left open the option of imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs if the UK joins the EU's Made in Europe scheme.
stories.summary: Downing Street has not ruled out imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles if the UK is admitted to the EU's Made in Europe package. A Franco-German proposal would require the UK to align with EU trade defence measures, including tariffs on Chinese EVs. Beijing has warned that such tariffs would be discriminatory. EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the legislation until late 2026 or early 2027.
key_points: Number 10 said it would welcome the UK being included in the Industrial Accelerator Act, after France dropped its opposition.

China's embassy in London called any discriminatory tariffs or restrictive measures unacceptable and said they breach WTO rules.

stories.story:
Downing Street has left open the possibility that the UK would impose tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as the price of joining the EU's Made in Europe package, formally the Industrial Accelerator Act. The government said it would welcome the UK being included after France dropped its opposition, but declined to say whether it accepted the tariff condition, calling it "premature to speculate" on terms.

A Franco-German proposal reported on Thursday would allow non-EU countries that were in the single market on 1 January 2020, including the UK and Norway, to opt in if they accept dynamic alignment with EU trade defence measures. The EU's 2024 tariffs on Chinese EVs would be part of that. The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, reportedly said the UK and EU should act in lockstep on China's automotive dominance, while the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said the UK would not be coerced. China's embassy said it was firmly opposed to discriminatory tariffs and that trade protectionism breaks WTO rules.

The stakes are significant. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, most to the EU, so the government is keen to avoid being locked out of EU supply chains. Tariffs could protect British manufacturers from cheap Chinese competition but could raise consumer prices and invite retaliation against UK car exports to China. Mercedes-Benz boss Ola Källenius has warned against excluding the UK, and Liam Byrne, chair of the business committee, has called tariffs a small price to pay. EU lawmakers have tabled 5,100 amendments and are expected to finalise the legislation by the end of 2026 or early 2027, so the outcome remains open.
stories.market_take: UK and European carmakers could benefit from protection against Chinese EVs, but a trade dispute with China could hurt exporters.

stories.story:
Iran is using public messaging to stress the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against it, timed ahead of the US midterm elections. Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets focusing on oil prices and the US economy. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's chief negotiator, has repeatedly attacked US officials over rising costs and military spending, including in a message to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

The economic background is stark. Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began on February 28, sending energy prices sharply higher. The American Automobile Association puts US diesel at an all-time record of $6.33 a gallon, and petrol at $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war. Inflation reportedly rose to 3.7% last month, and the Federal Reserve raised rates last month, despite Trump calling for cuts. stories.story:
A man described as a well-known individual is trying to obtain a permanent injunction to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing details of serious allegations against him. At a High Court hearing on Friday, his legal team argued there was a serious risk that he could harm himself if the allegations were made public.

The claimant's lawyers, led by Sara Mansoori KC, argue that publication would breach articles two and three of the European Convention on Human Rights, the first covering the right to life. They say he has attempted to take his own life twice and remains seriously ill. The allegations concern his conduct towards a number of individuals over several years in professional and personal settings. He has given a broad denial of them.

The Guardian and ITN, which conducted a journalistic investigation, are opposing the injunction. In a written argument they say the relevant human rights duties are not triggered and should not stop publication, and that any risks could be managed with safeguards. Mr Justice Nicklin said it was important that the proceedings remain as open as possible and that the case would be controversial whichever way it is decided.

A trial later this month will examine whether a ban on reporting should be made. The outcome will be watched closely for its implications for press freedom and for how courts weigh privacy and safety against publication.

stories.story:
Legal documents show that Thames Valley Police were concerned Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might delay officers entering his Sandringham home by arguing that the property belonged to King Charles. Police said such a delay could risk losing evidence, and they applied for search warrants on 18 February before searches of Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The former prince was arrested on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after the US Department of Justice published material linking him to Jeffrey Epstein. He has denied any wrongdoing relating to Epstein. The documents describe the police's wish to find paperwork and electronic devices connected to his time as a UK trade envoy, and mention claims about forwarding Epstein official reports and discussing investment opportunities.

Last week the High Court accepted that the search warrants were unlawful. The police said the court had issued them under the wrong section of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to challenge the force and the Central Criminal Court. Mountbatten-Windsor has described the police's concerns as speculation.

Despite the ruling, the judge said the investigation itself was not brought to an end and was not wholly unlawful. Items seized in the raid remain with the police, and a further hearing in 2027 will decide whether that material can be used as evidence. The criminal investigation is continuing.

For the wider market, the story matters because Treasury bills are a benchmark for short-term rates and a core holding for money market funds. Sustained weak auction demand could push yields higher and tighten financial conditions. The article does not say how the Treasury or the Fed might respond.

The settings menu explicitly warns that the feature increases battery use. The writer had switched it on expecting better video, and combined with heavy short-form video viewing, found the battery draining faster than usual. Online guides and forum users commonly recommend turning it off to save power. Estimates of the drain vary, with some suggesting it could reach about 2% per hour.

They could see little difference in smoothness when watching TikTok videos, though they acknowledge a side-by-side comparison might show a small change. They argue that people who use their phone for other tasks might value the higher refresh rate enough to accept the battery cost.

This is a personal experience piece rather than a formal test, so the figures are anecdotal. It is most useful for Pixel and Samsung owners who want to balance screen smoothness against battery endurance.

stories.headline: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
stories.claim: US Senate debates ahead of the 3 November midterms show heated exchanges and Republicans balancing loyalty to Trump.
stories.summary: A BBC analysis of recent US Senate debates ahead of the 3 November midterms highlights sharp personal attacks and the question of how closely Republican candidates align with President Trump. Trump's approval is reported as low, with voters concerned about the cost of living and fuel prices. Key races in Maine, Iowa, Michigan, Georgia and Texas are described, several of them unexpectedly close. Democrats need to flip four seats to gain control of the Senate.
key_points: Republican candidates face pressure over their alignment with Trump, and a Reuters analysis found two-thirds of competitive House and Senate candidates have broken with him in some way.
Susan Collins in Maine is running for a sixth term and says she has voted against Trump 137 times this Congress, with a close race against Troy Jackson.
In Iowa, Ashley Hinson faces a tougher-than-expected race against Josh Turek, with some polls showing him narrowly ahead.
In Michigan and Georgia, debates have featured personal attacks, including comments about the Muslim background of Abdul El-Sayed and remarks involving Mike Collins's family.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win against Ken Paxton, but Paxton has not accepted any debate invitations.
Democrats need to flip one of four seats to take control of the Senate, and 21 of 35 seats up for election have no scheduled main-candidate debates.
stories.story:
With the US midterm elections due on 3 November, Senate candidates have been holding debates that have featured sharp exchanges and personal attacks. The BBC reports that a central theme is how closely Republicans align with President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings have been low in recent months. Polling suggests voters are most concerned about the cost of living and high fuel prices. A Reuters analysis cited in the piece found that around two-thirds of candidates in competitive House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this cycle.

Several races are described as unexpectedly tight. In Maine, Republican Susan Collins, who is seeking a sixth term, has distanced herself from Trump and is facing Democrat Troy Jackson. Polls vary, with one mid-September New York Times/Siena poll suggesting Collins could be ahead by 3 points while others show Jackson leading. In Iowa, Republican Ashley Hinson is facing Democrat Josh Turek, with some polls suggesting Turek has a narrow lead. Hinson has criticised a Trump administration deal to import Russian fuel, while still largely backing the president.

Debates have also been marked by personal insults. In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers questioned whether members of the family of his Muslim opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, might be on a watchlist, and El-Sayed hit back strongly. In Georgia, incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff and Republican Mike Collins traded insults, and a social media controversy involving Collins's son-in-law has become an issue. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has accepted four debate invitations but Republican Ken Paxton has accepted none, despite Trump urging the candidates to debate.

The piece notes that 21 of the 35 Senate seats up for grabs have no scheduled debates among the main candidates, according to an ABC News analysis. stories.story:
A new survey commissioned by Clean Energy Canada suggests that Canadian electric vehicle buyers are holding off on purchases while they wait for more Chinese models to reach the market. Of the 48% of respondents who said they were likely to buy an EV as their next vehicle, 42% said they wanted to wait for more Chinese EVs to become available. The survey points to growing interest in EVs overall, but a clear preference for Chinese brands over Western options currently on sale.

The shift follows an agreement between Canada and China under which up to 49,000 Chinese EVs can be imported each year. The deal was linked to a trade dispute over canola, with China dropping its tariffs on the crop in return. Canada had previously matched a US-style 100% tariff on Chinese EVs. Only about 16,000 Chinese EVs have been brought in so far, and the article reports that Tesla has already reached its allocation because it had distribution networks in place. Other brands are still setting up distribution and are expected to bring more models next year.

The article notes that Canadian sentiment towards US brands has soured, partly because of tariffs imposed by Washington, and that some Western automakers have cancelled EV models. Gas prices are also high, which could encourage buyers to switch to electric cars. The writer, however, is strongly critical of US policy and of American automakers, and includes personal opinion that goes beyond the survey. Those judgements should be read as commentary rather than reported fact.

The key question is whether Chinese brands can build networks and supply enough models quickly enough to meet demand. If they can, the deal could reshape the Canadian EV market and add pressure on Western automakers that have been slow to compete on price and technology.
stories.market_take: Chinese EV import access into Canada could add competitive pressure on Tesla and Western carmakers, though volumes are still small.

stories.story:
Five web data-scraping and proxy brands have been formally brought together under a single name, Source, based in Vilnius, Lithuania. The brands are Oxylabs, Decodo, Webshare, ScrapingBee and Honeygain. According to the group, the move reflects demand from AI agents, next-generation search tools and frontier AI products that pull live data from the web. The group says demand across its companies has grown fourfold in a year and that its systems now handle 1.5 million requests per second.

Source describes itself as a shared back office rather than a business in its own right. It handles patents, procurement, hiring and compliance, while each brand retains its own team, product strategy and customer base. The brands are split by customer type: Oxylabs serves enterprises and AI labs, Decodo targets mid-market firms, ScrapingBee sells developer interfaces, Webshare serves individual professionals, and Honeygain pays users for spare bandwidth. The group is also expanding into web search interfaces designed for AI agents.

The article notes that the firms were already closely linked. Oxylabs bought Webshare in 2022 and ScrapingBee in 2025, and Honeygain became a key residential proxy partner in 2021. Source's chief executive, Vytautas Savickas, led Decodo until March 2026 before moving to Oxylabs, and the company's founder became chairman. The writer suggests the new group is a marriage of convenience rather than a true merger, and points out that several of these brands are reviewed as alternatives to one another.

Legal history is part of the context. Reddit sued Oxylabs and others in October 2025, alleging they bypassed its anti-scraping measures to take content from Google search results. Oxylabs has said it was shocked and would defend itself. A Texas jury had also previously awarded a rival nearly $7.5 million against Oxylabs in a 2021 patent case. The new search products may be an extension of existing offerings rather than an entirely new line.
stories.market_take: Source is privately held, so there is no direct listed stock to move on this news.

stories.claim: US Representative Ritchie Torres proposed the Power to Players Act, which would require game purchases to give lasting ownership and offline play.

The bill directs the Federal Trade Commission to act against cases such as NBA 2K25 becoming unplayable after server shutdowns. It would require normally online-only games to offer offline modes. stories.story:
US Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from New York, has proposed a bill called the Power to Players Act. It aims to set rules so that buying a video game gives the buyer ownership of the game rather than a licence to play it. The bill would also seek to ensure buyers can keep accessing games for years after release, and it directs the Federal Trade Commission to act against situations like the one affecting NBA 2K25.

NBA 2K25 launched on 6 September 2025 but is set to become unplayable on 31 December because its servers are being shut down. Torres said a game that can be removed when a company stops supporting it is effectively a rental. He told Kotaku that the aim was a return to the historical norm of the 1990s, when games were generally owned outright. According to the report, the bill would require normally online-only games to offer offline modes, although it does not appear to require servers to stay online indefinitely.

The proposal comes as consumers protest Sony's plan to stop releasing PlayStation games on physical media. Sony's earnings report said digital downloads made up 82% of full-game unit sales on PS4 and PS5. The article notes that physical discs do not fully solve the issue, since many disc games still need online servers and licence agreements usually grant revocable licences.

The bill has a long way to go, and its full text is not yet available, so its effectiveness cannot be judged. Offline modes could also be technically difficult for some online games. The article also notes that large language models have enabled many unofficial decompilation projects, which are probably illegal but hard to enforce.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market impact; a rule requiring offline modes could raise development costs for publishers with online-only games.

The reviewer found it very quick and well handled, but says it blends in visually. The test car cost $149,610 with options, against a starting price of $112,700. The review also flags the navigation system's confusing charging suggestions and questions some optional extras.
key_points: The 2026 Macan Turbo EV has 630 horsepower and a 100 kWh battery.
The starting price is $112,700, while the reviewed car cost $149,610 with options and fees.
The reviewer reports about 285 miles of highway range and fast charging from 19% to 80% in 20 minutes.
Acceleration and handling, including four-wheel steering, are praised.
The navigation system's charging directions were judged underwhelming.
stories.story:
TechCrunch has published a review of the 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV, an electric version of Porsche's compact crossover. The reviewer, who used the car for a week, says it looks like a family SUV and does not attract the attention that sports cars usually do. The article asks what a sports car should look like, and suggests that the Macan's performance is what makes it a sports car at heart.

The review praises the acceleration, which the reviewer says feels dramatic even at motorway speeds, and the four-wheel steering, which makes the car feel responsive on winding roads. The car has 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. It starts at $112,700, but the car tested cost $149,610 including destination fees and options such as a head-up display, large wheels and a premium sound system. The reviewer reports about 285 miles of highway range and a fast charge from 19% to 80% in 20 minutes on a 350-kilowatt charger.

The review is less positive about some aspects. The navigation system sent the reviewer to two chargers in sequence, which the reviewer found confusing, and the car continued to direct them to a slower charger after they had already reached a fast one. The reviewer also suggests skipping several costly options, such as the passenger display and decorative lighting. The article also notes that EVs cannot technically have turbochargers, though the name is kept for branding reasons.

The piece is a product review rather than news, and it offers no broader market or policy consequences.

stories.headline: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
stories.claim: Brazilian Amazon deforestation fell 41.8% in the past year to a record low, ahead of a 25 October presidential run-off.
stories.summary: Official satellite data show Amazon deforestation fell 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest since records began in 1988. The result is a boost for President Lula da Silva, who faces Flávio Bolsonaro in the 25 October run-off. The Cerrado savannah also recorded its lowest annual deforestation since 2001. Conservationists say the outcome of the election will determine whether the trend continues.
key_points: Amazon deforestation fell 41.8% to 3,335 sq km, the lowest figure since 1988.
Deforestation has slowed by 71.2% since 2022, the year before Lula's administration began.
Cerrado deforestation was 5,516 sq km, its lowest since 2001.
The run-off between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro is on 25 October.
Conservationists warn that the election result will determine future forest protection.
stories.story:
Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, according to new government data. The Prodes satellite series, which is widely regarded as the most accurate measure, shows clearance fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres. This is 1,236 sq km below the previous record low. The figures were compiled by Brazil's National Institute for Space Research.

The result is a success for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose government has slowed deforestation by 71.2% since 2022. The decline was attributed mainly to stronger enforcement and greater state investment in environmental agencies. The Cerrado savannah also recorded its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km, and has fallen by 48.4% over four years. Pará, Mato Grosso and Amazonas had the highest shares of clearance, though all three were down by more than 45%. Roraima was the only state where deforestation rose, by 0.4%.

The outcome of the presidential run-off on 25 October is now crucial. Lula fell behind in the first round against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The article contrasts this record with the 2019–2023 period under Jair Bolsonaro, when Amazon deforestation rose by 59.5%, due to weaker protection agencies and fewer penalties. Jair Bolsonaro was later convicted of attempting a coup, and his son has pledged to free him.

The candidates differ sharply on relations with the United States and on environmental policy. Lula has warned against US pressure on Brazil's resources, while the Bolsonaro family has close ties to the Trump administration and may shift trade priorities towards the US, particularly for critical minerals. Conservation groups say the data shows that ending deforestation is achievable but depends on the election.
stories.market_take: The run-off could shift Brazil's trade and resource policy, relevant to commodity and currency investors.

stocks.reason: The election outcome could affect Brazil's policy direction and investor sentiment.

stories.claim: Google has begun rolling out Universal Cart, a shopping cart feature across Search, Chrome, AI Mode and Gemini in the US.
stories.summary: Google has started rolling out Universal Cart in the US, placing a shopping cart icon prominently across Search, AI Mode, desktop Chrome and the Gemini app. The feature was previewed at I/O 2026 as a hub for shopping. stories.story:
Google has started rolling out Universal Cart, which it describes as an intelligent shopping cart and a hub for shopping across its products. The feature was first previewed at Google's I/O 2026 developer event in May. It is currently being released in the United States and is appearing in several places at once, including Google Search, AI Mode, desktop Chrome's new tab page, the Gemini app and the Google app on Android.

The cart lets users save products from multiple retailers in one place. It tracks stock availability and sends price drop notifications. At checkout, it surfaces available promo codes and highlights which payment method in Google Wallet offers the best perks. Some retailers, including Nike, Target, Walmart and Shopify merchants, allow purchases to be completed directly within Google's interface, and product pages gain an Add to cart button.

The reviewer at 9to5Google, while noting the usefulness of the price tracking and checkout features, argued that the cart icon is perhaps too prominent. They said it makes ordinary search results look like a store page, which they found jarring on first use.

The rollout signals Google's continued push to keep shopping activity within its own products, as it competes with retailers and other platforms for purchase journeys. The feature depends on the Universal Commerce Protocol. Further adoption across retailers and countries would determine how significant the change becomes for e-commerce.
stories.market_take: A modest positive for Google's commerce ambitions, with some pressure on retailers and payment platforms that lose direct traffic.

stories.headline: AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push
stories.claim: AOC transferred $1m from her campaign to support Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ahead of the November midterms.
stories.summary: US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1 million from her own campaign to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, backing progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. She confirmed the donation in a statement and at events in Michigan, including Detroit. The move comes as the Michigan Senate race, one of the key contests for control of the chamber, has become one of the most expensive in the state's history. El-Sayed currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points in a polling average.
key_points: Ocasio-Cortez transferred $1m from her own campaign to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, first reported by the New York Times.
She framed the support as a response to attacks on El-Sayed's Muslim faith, Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine.
El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 points in a Real Clear Politics average of high-quality polls.

stories.story:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1 million from her own campaign to support Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive candidate running for the US Senate in Michigan. She confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and during a speech in the Detroit area. She said she was giving the money to show that help was on its way and pointed to attacks on El-Sayed that focus on his Muslim faith, Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine. The money went to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, and the New York Times first reported the transfer.

The donation follows a campaign appearance by Ocasio-Cortez in Michigan, where she joined El-Sayed on a bus tour of the Upper Peninsula and held three events in Detroit. The pair focused on economic issues. Polling averages show El-Sayed ahead of Rogers by 2.6 points, and the race has become one of the most expensive in the state's history, with spending topping $268m as of October 15. El-Sayed outraised Rogers over the summer, bringing in $30.6m against $9.6m, although Rogers held more cash on hand at the end of September.

The article places the race within a wider national picture. Donald Trump's approval ratings are reported to be at a low ahead of the midterms, and recent polls suggest many Americans want substantial change in how the country is run. Progressive Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to invest more equally in progressive candidates, including El-Sayed. El-Sayed has also won support from Bernie Sanders, who donated $250,000, and from more centrist figures such as Barack Obama and Kamala Harris. Michigan is among the Senate races that could determine which party controls the chamber in the final two years of Trump's term.

Cobb County police's major crimes unit and Georgia authorities are still investigating.
Six Flags has temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six US amusement parks since the death.
stories.story:
The family of a man who died after being ejected from a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, near Atlanta, has questioned whether the death could have been prevented. Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was riding the Goliath with his niece during a family trip to celebrate her birthday when he was thrown from the ride. Details were reported by local broadcaster WSB-TV.

His brother-in-law, Joshua Nelson, said the family largely believed it was a freak accident but was also asking whether it could have been avoided. Nelson relayed an account from his daughter, who was seated beside Kariem, saying he appeared to faint or pass out, and that his safety latch may have snapped or come loose as the ride rose again. These are the family's accounts of what the witness described, not established findings.

Kariem was an educator and the father of a ten-year-old daughter. He had begun his career as a technology teacher at Wesley International Academy before becoming an information technology manager, according to Atlanta Public Schools.

Georgia authorities were still investigating the circumstances as of Friday, and the Cobb County police department's major crimes unit has opened an inquiry. Six Flags has temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six of its US parks since the death. The cause of the incident has not been officially determined.

stories.claim: A New Jersey deputy attorney general has been arrested on charges tied to AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
stories.summary: Brian Richard Fitzgerald, a deputy attorney general in New Jersey since 2016, was arrested by Bucks County detectives on felony charges linked to AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Police say he used AI to turn photos of real minors taken from social media into sexualised images and shared them online. Detectives recovered prompts and scripts used to make the images and Discord chats in which he allegedly admitted making and sharing them. He faces charges including possession and dissemination of CSAM and criminal use of a communication facility. The case is rare because the accused works for the state's top law enforcement office.
key_points: Brian Richard Fitzgerald, 51, a New Jersey deputy attorney general, was arrested on felony charges linked to AI-generated CSAM.
Bucks County detectives said the arrest followed a search and that prompts, scripts and Discord chat logs were recovered.

stories.story:
A New Jersey deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, has been arrested on felony charges relating to AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Bucks County detectives announced the arrest in a press release on Thursday. Fitzgerald, who is 51, is accused of using artificial intelligence to alter photographs of real children taken from social media into sexualised images, and then sharing those images on social media.

According to the police statement, a search on Thursday uncovered prompts and scripts used to generate the material with an AI program. Investigators also reviewed Discord chat logs in which a user with a name linked to Fitzgerald allegedly admitted to making several illicit images and sharing them with other users. He has been charged with possession of child sexual abuse material, dissemination of such material and criminal use of a communication facility.

Fitzgerald's LinkedIn profile says he has been a deputy attorney general since 2016, handling insurance fraud and insurance licensee cases as a state prosecutor. The case is unusual because the accused works within the office responsible for state law enforcement and legal affairs. The article notes that US authorities have pursued AI-generated abuse material since at least 2024, when the Justice Department brought one of its early cases and said that such material is still CSAM. Other recent cases include a Pennsylvania police officer arrested earlier this year for making AI pornography from driver's licence photos, and a Korean police officer accused of making AI pornography including CSAM.

New Jersey's district attorney, Joe Khan, said in a statement that the state agrees with the Justice Department that AI-generated abuse material is as harmful as other such material. He said the office would pursue these cases aggressively regardless of the offender's profession. The case will now move through the courts, where the charges will be tested.

stories.headline: 32,768 cores and 74 petaflops: AMD’s monster new rack for AI agents could be too much for traditional data centers
stories.claim: AMD is developing the Helion Agentic AI Rack, a rack-scale system for AI agents due in November 2026, that may strain traditional data centres.
stories.summary: AMD has outlined the Helion Agentic AI Rack, a rack-scale system for AI agents with configurations for personal, enterprise and technical workloads. It supports up to 32,768 Zen 6 CPU cores, 16 Instinct MI350P accelerators, 74 petaflops of FP4 compute and 102 Tbps of networking. The article argues that existing data centres may lack the power, cooling and networking needed. Availability is scheduled for November 2026, though costs were not disclosed.
key_points: The Helion Agentic AI Rack supports up to 32,768 Zen 6 CPU cores and 16 Instinct MI350P accelerators.

stories.story:
AMD is developing a rack-scale computing system aimed at artificial intelligence agents, called the Helion Agentic AI Rack. The platform is designed in several configurations for personal assistants, enterprise applications and technical computing. It can support up to 32,768 Zen 6 x86 CPU cores, 16 Instinct MI350P accelerators, 74 petaflops of FP4 computing performance and 102 Tbps of networking bandwidth.

The design varies by use. Personal agent setups use 256-core Venice processors at 400W, focused on density and efficiency. Enterprise setups use the same 256-core chips rated at 600W, with separate nodes for agent execution, inference and general computing. Technical workloads use 96-core, higher-frequency Venice processors. The enterprise version pairs CPUs with graphics accelerators, and the system includes an integrated token router to direct model requests across frontier and open-source models.

The article argues that many existing data centres may not be suited to this hardware. Facilities built around standard cloud or legacy enterprise servers may lack enough power delivery, cooling and network capacity, and mixing different server types adds planning complexity. Operators may need to upgrade infrastructure to cope with the high-core-count and networking demands.

The rack is scheduled to become available in November 2026. AMD has not yet disclosed the full cost of facility upgrades or the cooling requirements, so the practical cost of deployment remains unclear.
stories.market_take: A product announcement with a November 2026 launch; it may help AMD's data centre pitch but has no immediate financial effect.

stocks.reason: The company is the developer of the rack and gains a product for AI agent workloads.

stories.headline: LG's next-gen OLED tech is coming to laptops and monitors first, and we've got a rough timeline
stories.claim: LG Display is developing a mask-free OLED patterning method called FLiPP, aiming for mass production of monitors by late 2027.
stories.summary: LG Display is developing a mask-free OLED manufacturing process called FLiPP, which it says raises production efficiency. Reported figures show material utilisation rising sharply and gains in brightness, lifetime or power use. The company expects mass production to begin around late 2027, starting with monitors before laptops.
key_points: FLiPP removes fine metal masks from OLED manufacturing and uses photolithography and etching instead.
LG Display reports material utilisation rising from 75% to over 93%, according to The Elec.
The process could improve luminance by 1.6x, lifetime by 2.4x, or cut power use by 13%.
The technology is still in the first development stage, with mass production targeted by late 2027.
stories.story:
LG Display is developing a new method for making OLED panels called FLiPP, which stands for FMM-Less innovative Pixel Patterning. Conventional OLED manufacturing uses fine metal masks to place the organic light-emitting materials precisely. FLiPP skips the mask: materials are deposited across the glass, given a protective layer, and then refined using photolithography and etching to remove unwanted areas.

According to figures LG Display reported to trade site The Elec and cited by TechRadar, the method raised utilisation of production from 75% to over 93%. Utilisation of the organic emissive materials rose from 40% to 74%, and the pixel aperture ratio reached 65%. The figures were recorded on 23.5-inch panels. The technology could be used to increase brightness by 1.6 times, extend longevity by 2.4 times, or reduce power consumption by 13%.

LG Display's chief technology officer, Choi Young-seok, says the technology is at an early development stage, with product development and mass production to follow. The company expects to reach mass production by late 2027, initially for monitors and later possibly laptops, which could mean first products around CES 2028. The head of its next-generation display division, Cho Heung-ryeol, said the company is assessing whether existing LCD and WOLED lines can be reused without major changes or whether new plant is needed.

The article suggests the first devices will be monitors and laptops rather than televisions, so TV buyers should not expect quick price cuts from this technology. The timeline is still early, and the efficiency gains are reported on a single panel size.
stories.market_take: Efficiency gains could benefit LG Display over time, though production timelines remain distant.

stocks.reason: Improved production efficiency could lower costs if the process reaches mass production.

stories.summary: Federal prosecutors in New York have charged Moises Freire with rape and distributing fentanyl with intent to commit rape after a student at the Fashion Institute of Technology died from the drug. A second man, Brian Peralta Cabrera, faces a drug conspiracy charge, and a third, Harry Rosales Pino, has already pleaded guilty. The victim's friend also nearly died. The superseding charges were filed on Thursday, and the defendants remain in federal custody. The case highlights the fentanyl crisis and campus safety.
key_points: Moises Freire, 19, faces charges of conspiracy to distribute fentanyl and distributing a deadly drug with intent to rape.
Prosecutors say he told two women the fentanyl was cocaine, and one died after a coma on 21 March.
Brian Peralta Cabrera, 18, is charged in the drug conspiracy; Harry Rosales Pino pleaded guilty in September.
Prosecutors allege Freire sent photos of the women while they were unconscious and waited about 40 minutes before alerting security.
FIT's president said Narcan kits are in residence hall lobbies and public safety staff must now carry them.
All defendants have pleaded not guilty to earlier charges; the new charges have not yet been arraigned.
stories.story:
Federal prosecutors in New York say a 19-year-old man, Moises Freire, gave fentanyl to two students at the Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) and raped one of them while she was unconscious. The student later went into a coma and died on 21 March. Her friend overdosed and nearly died. The US Department of Justice announced the updated charges on Thursday, which add the rape allegation against Freire. Prosecutors say he was not a student at FIT but visited the dormitory room and falsely described the drug as pure cocaine, even though he had reportedly called it 'straight poison'.

Two other men are also charged. Brian Peralta Cabrera, 18, faces a count of conspiracy to distribute fentanyl. Harry Rosales Pino pleaded guilty in September to plotting to distribute narcotics resulting in death and serious bodily injury, and is due to be sentenced on 15 December. Prosecutors allege the fentanyl passed from Rosales to Peralta and then to Freire. All three had earlier pleaded not guilty to initial charges that did not include the rape allegation. Freire and Peralta had not been arraigned on the new charges and remain in federal custody.

At an April hearing, an assistant US attorney described how Freire had allegedly admitted in writing to having sex with the unconscious woman, and then photographed the women while they were passed out. Prosecutors said he did not call an ambulance and that a friend had warned him the drug 'doesn't look like coke'. The women were taken to hospital after security was alerted.

FIT president Jason Schupbach said the charges reflected a 'horrific tragedy' and pointed to safety measures on campus, including Narcan kits in residence lobbies and a requirement for public safety staff to carry the overdose reversal drug. The university said it would keep the community informed while protecting the privacy of the victims and families. The case reflects the wider danger of fentanyl, which the US government identifies as a major driver of drug deaths.

stories.headline: Meta employees say Lula’s accounts restricted in Brazil election: Report
stories.claim: Meta employees reportedly acknowledged that Lula's Instagram accounts were restricted and Bolsonaro's profile was recommended during Brazil's election.
stories.summary: Folha de S Paulo reports that internal Meta messages acknowledge Brazilian President Lula's Instagram accounts were negatively affected by restrictions, and that the platform recommended rival Flavio Bolsonaro's profile and WhatsApp channel. Meta says the issues were already public and concern severity, not political interference. A Brazilian court has ordered Meta to treat both candidates equally ahead of the 25 October runoff, with daily fines for non-compliance.
key_points: Folha de S Paulo says internal Meta messages acknowledge Lula's Instagram accounts were negatively affected.
The messages reportedly say Bolsonaro's profile and WhatsApp channel were recommended by the platform.
Meta says the technical issues were already public and the conversations concerned their severity, not politics.
A Brazilian electoral court judge ordered Meta to ensure equal treatment, with fines of 500,000 reais per day for non-compliance.
The presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro is due on 25 October.
stories.story:
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo has reported that Meta employees acknowledged in internal messages that Instagram accounts of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were negatively affected by restrictions during the election. The paper said the messages also acknowledged that the platform recommended the profile of challenger Flavio Bolsonaro and his WhatsApp channel. Folha said it reviewed the messages, and the report was published on Friday.

Meta told Reuters that the technical issues cited were already public and that the conversations concerned how severe those issues were, not political interference. The company said any suggestion that it favours one side is false. The row comes ahead of a presidential runoff on 25 October, in which Lula will face Bolsonaro after the senator performed better than expected in the first round.

The report followed a ruling on Thursday by a judge at Brazil's top electoral court. The judge ordered Meta to act immediately to treat both candidates equally. The ruling bars Meta from reducing political content distribution, restricting searches or removing posts in a way that creates imbalance, and requires its AI tool to apply identical criteria to both candidates. Failure to comply carries a fine of 500,000 reais, about $98,700, per day. The order came after Lula filed a complaint accusing the company of biased algorithms and AI restrictions.

Lula's party says some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach, with reaction, sharing, audio and speed options missing. The situation raises questions about platform neutrality in elections and could lead to further regulatory action. Meta owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
stories.market_take: Regulatory pressure and daily fines in Brazil are a modest risk for Meta, though the amounts are small relative to its size.

stocks.reason: Regulatory pressure and potential fines in Brazil could weigh on the company.

stories.headline: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
stories.claim: Chancellor John Healey says there is a pro-growth case for a Heathrow third runway, despite PM Andy Burnham's reluctance.
stories.summary: Chancellor John Healey has argued that there is a pro-growth case for building a third runway at Heathrow, even though Prime Minister Andy Burnham has not backed the project. Healey said the government will study responses to a recently closed public consultation. Burnham has reportedly said the runway should be a matter for London and Londoners, and a Sunday Times report said he was unconvinced. Heathrow's chief executive warned that shareholders could reassess their backing if the project does not get the prime minister's support. The decision on a planning application is expected in the coming months, and Healey's 28 October budget is approaching.
key_points: Healey said airports have been a big part of jobs and growth, and the case for the Heathrow runway is a case for growth.
Burnham has avoided taking a clear position since becoming prime minister in July.
A recent Sunday Times report said Burnham told the transport secretary he was unconvinced by the project.

The IMF praised the UK's deficit-cutting action, and official figures showed the economy grew unexpectedly in August.
stories.story:
Chancellor John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow, despite the prime minister, Andy Burnham, declining to back the project. Speaking in Bangkok, where he attended the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation that has recently closed. He said airports across the UK have been a major source of jobs and growth, and that the case for the Heathrow runway has always rested on growth.

The position contrasts with that of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who made approval of the runway a central part of her growth speech last year. Since entering Downing Street in July, Burnham has avoided the question, suggesting it should be a matter for London and Londoners. A recent Sunday Times report said he had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was unconvinced by the arguments for the scheme.

Heathrow's chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that shareholders could reassess their support for the £33bn infrastructure project if the prime minister does not back it. The airport's owners include Qatar's investment authority, the French firm Ardian, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Singapore's GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.

Healey, who voted for the runway in the Commons in 2018, has returned to London to finalise his 28 October budget. The IMF praised the UK for cutting its deficit, and its managing director urged him to stay the course. Separately, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly kept growing in August.
stories.market_take: The runway debate matters mainly for Heathrow's owners and UK infrastructure sentiment, with limited direct effect on broader markets.

stories.story:

He said Replit uses an internal benchmark and also publishes a public one.

The claim has been questioned. An insider familiar with the arrangement, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. A September blog post also referred to Anthropic models running in Replit's agent production environment. TechCrunch said it had asked Replit for clarification and would update the story if it responded.

Replit sells a cloud-based platform that lets users build and deploy apps from a browser. Under the Anthropic arrangement, it used Claude models to run the platform, and that partnership had reportedly helped drive strong revenue growth. Replit announced an OpenAI partnership in August. Masad said enterprise contracts were about 15% of revenue this year, compared with 2% last year, and that more than half of revenue now comes from business customers. He did not share annual recurring revenue figures.

Masad also spoke about AI safety, saying agents need a proper 'habitat' that includes good orchestration, error recovery, security, sandboxing, networking and identity controls before they can be deployed safely.

stories.story:
A developer planning a data centre in Cardiff has said it is also seeking permission for a gas-fired power plant to help get the site running. The proposal, from Curtis Hall, is for a site currently used as a park and ride serving the University Hospital of Wales. The developer says the gas plant could operate for up to five years if the site cannot connect to the national grid quickly enough. It described the gas plan as a worst-case scenario included in the planning documents to test the upper limit of emissions and noise.

The planning documents describe a temporary energy centre with gas turbines capable of generating up to 49.9MW, just below the 50MW level that would require Welsh government permission. The centre would start in July 2028 and run until the site has a full grid connection, expected around July 2033. The data centre itself would eventually need 150MW from the grid, which may not be delivered until between 2030 and 2034. Once connected, around 40 diesel backup generators would also be needed to ensure continuous power. The developer denied it was trying to avoid a Welsh government application by setting the capacity at 49.9MW.

Opposition has been strong. Friends of the Earth Cymru called the proposal climate-wrecking infrastructure, and most local Senedd members have formally objected, along with a Welsh government minister and a senior Labour councillor on Cardiff Council. Residents of a nearby housing estate have raised concerns about noise, pollution and the effect on hospital staff and patients. The developer says the site would not be audible locally and that air quality effects are not significant. It also points to benefits such as a new road bridge and jobs.

The Welsh government is considering whether to take over the planning process, which would prevent Cardiff Council from granting permission in the meantime. The government also plans to publish its own policy on data centres by the end of the year. The debate reflects wider controversy over the electricity demands of data centres, which have grown with interest in artificial intelligence.

stories.headline: The Leap Second Is No More
stories.claim: The BIPM has decided to stop issuing leap seconds from May 2027, with a leap hour considered only for the distant future.
stories.summary: The International Bureau of Weights and Measurements has agreed to stop adding leap seconds to Coordinated Universal Time from May 2027. The decision removes the risk of a first negative leap second, which experts said could cause disruption. Time will instead keep accumulating, and a future leap hour has been discussed for the far future.
key_points: The BIPM will stop issuing leap seconds from May 2027, with the change dated to May 20, 2027.
Thirty-two leap seconds have been added to UTC since 1972.
Concerns about a negative leap second, which had never been tested, drove the decision.
Some tech systems, including those run by Google and Meta, smear leap seconds over a day, while others such as Qantas's booking system have failed.
stories.story:
The International Bureau of Weights and Measurements (BIPM) has announced that it will stop issuing leap seconds to adjust Coordinated Universal Time from May 2027. Since 1972, 32 leap seconds have been added to keep atomic time in line with the Earth's slowing rotation. The most recent was added in 2016. The change was announced on a Thursday and the chosen date is May 20, 2027, the anniversary of the Metre Convention and Metrology Day.

The main reason for the decision is concern about a negative leap second, which would remove a second rather than add one. Officials said positive leap seconds have caused continuing problems for decades and that negative ones had never been properly tested. A standards group reportedly found several failures in tests of a negative leap, adding urgency. A 2024 study in Nature suggested a negative leap second could be needed as early as 2029, partly because melting ice has changed the planet's rotation.

For technology, the change removes a recurring source of disruption. Many systems rely on UTC for timestamps and databases, and past leap seconds have caused errors, such as a 2012 booking system failure at Qantas. Companies have used methods such as smearing, spreading the extra second over a day, but these are not uniform across the industry.

Atomic and astronomical time will still drift apart over the long run, so the BIPM has also agreed to create a leap hour for the future. Officials said it is millennia away and that systems relying on UTC will need no action, while those using UT1 will need to handle differences larger than one second.
stories.market_take: The change is technical and unlikely to move markets, though it may matter for firms that run time-sensitive systems.

sources.title: The Leap Second Is No More

stories.story:
Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Argon, which scored 97.5% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, a test widely seen as demanding for general problem-solving. The result was achieved using a test setup called the Provider Adapter Harness, which uses vendor-specific features such as retained reasoning and context compaction. ARC Prize said Google is now the second lab after OpenAI to exceed 95% on the benchmark. GPT-6 Astra scored higher at 99.9%.

The article stresses that results depend heavily on test conditions. Under the Standard Harness, which allows only simple notes between rounds, Argon fell to 49.8% at low reasoning, at a cost of $5,800. API problems meant it completed only some of the 55 games, and the highest reasoning setting did not yield a published score. The reporting also describes an earlier dispute in July 2026 over how OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 were tested, which showed how much setup can change outcomes.

Epoch AI's Capabilities Index, which combines more than 50 benchmarks, puts Argon at 165 points. That ties Fable 5.1 and sits just behind Opus 5.5 at 167 and GPT-6 Astra at 166. Argon is well ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash at 157, and the article says Google is closer to the frontier than at any point since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February.

Performance is uneven by domain. Epoch estimates Argon is eighth on the maths index and sixth on the software engineering index, even though it leads several knowledge, agent and vision benchmarks. Readers should treat headline benchmark numbers with caution.

stories.headline: How does the new Tesla Roadster 'fly', and is it dangerous to be around its thrusters?
stories.claim: Tesla's Roadster was unveiled with SpaceX-derived cold-gas thrusters, and the Rocket version is not approved for public roads.
stories.summary: At a showcase, Tesla unveiled the new Roadster, with a claimed top speed above 230mph and cold-gas thrusters borrowed from SpaceX. The top Rocket version carries up to 10 thrusters and is sold by invite only. Tesla's website marks the Rocket version as not approved for public road use. The Performance version, with production planned for 2028, has no thrusters. Analysts raise safety concerns about the thrust force.
key_points: The Rocket variant uses up to 10 thrusters powered by compressed-air tanks, with up to 600 litres of air.
Tesla says the four rear thrusters alone produce over 80 kilonewtons of force.
The Rocket version is marked 'not approved for public road use' on Tesla's website.
The Thrust version is labelled a limited release, while the Performance version is road ready.
Musk said the car was 'not necessarily a safety optimized car' and that road legality 'depends on the street'.
The next demonstration is planned for the Idaho Snake River Canyon.
stories.story:
Tesla has unveiled its long-delayed Roadster, and the showcase focused on the car's ability to leap, hover briefly and flip using thrusters borrowed from SpaceX. Tesla claims a top speed of more than 230mph and 0-60mph in under 0.59 seconds. The top Rocket version can be fitted with up to 10 thrusters and will be available by invite only. In the demonstrations, the car, which had no driver and was controlled autonomously, went upside down, flipped back and jumped over a line of parked vehicles.

The thrusters are cold-gas units, meaning they release highly compressed air rather than burning fuel. Tesla says the Rocket variant can hold a maximum of 600 litres of air across tanks, including a 200-litre tank for the rear thrusters and a 400-litre tank that replaces the passenger seat. Tesla says the car can refill its tanks on its own, although how long that takes is not known. Electric motors open and close the thrusters to make small adjustments in flight.

The article's author says the thrust is so strong that it would be dangerous to people and vehicles nearby, and that exhaust gas at supersonic speed could hurl debris. Musk himself was not confident about road use. The Rocket version is clearly labelled as not approved for public roads, the Thrust version is a limited release, and the Performance version, reservable now for production planned in 2028, is road ready without thrusters.

For now, the flying Roadster appears to be a showcase car rather than something likely to be used on public roads. The next demonstration is planned for the Idaho Snake River Canyon, a site associated with Evel Knievel.
stories.market_take: The showcase may draw attention to Tesla, but the article gives no direct share price impact.

stocks.reason: Strong attention from the showcase, but the Rocket version has limited road approval and sales.

Some employees had been spending as much as $1,000 a month. Extra use must be charged to a project budget code, and Claude access is reviewed periodically. An Accenture spokesperson said the company continues to invest in AI.
key_points: The $29 monthly cap replaces spending that in some cases reached $1,000 a month.
Usage above the cap must be charged to a Work Breakdown Structure, Accenture's project budget code.
Premium plans include $250 of token usage a week, while many staff are on the General plan.

stories.story:
Accenture has limited how much its employees can spend on Claude, the AI model developed by Anthropic. According to an internal announcement seen by 404 Media, staff now have a monthly allowance of $29 per person, with any extra use charged to a project budget code. The change took effect on 1 October. Some employees had previously been spending as much as $1,000 a month on the tool.

Under the new arrangements, usage above the $29 has to be charged to a Work Breakdown Structure, which Accenture uses to track specific projects or teams. Premium plans include $250 of token usage a week, but many staff are on the General plan. The announcement also says that Claude Enterprise access depends on role and business need and that licences will be reviewed from time to time. Some employees have asked for premium accounts to keep project costs down, and one said their usage had been above $500 a month. Another employee reported that their access had been removed entirely.

An Accenture spokesperson said the company makes AI available to all its people and that its approach is to use the right tool for each job. The company, which has about 799,000 people, recently invested in the AI platform Within. A survey cited in the announcement found that 82% of more than 3,000 executives plan to increase AI investment. 404 Media noted the irony of Accenture urging clients to invest heavily in AI while restricting its own staff.

The move reflects a wider trend, as other companies have started to cap employee AI spending. Microsoft set AI budgets for its divisions in August, Atlassian has introduced an AI budget for its engineers, and Uber's technology chief has said the era of heavy AI token use is ending.
stories.market_take: Tighter AI usage budgets at large consultancies could slightly reduce near-term AI tool spending by enterprise staff.

stories.summary: On its earnings call, Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster confirmed the firm plans to launch its own version of the tax-aware long/short strategy. Such products have grown rapidly, with assets reportedly rising from $2 billion in 2022 to more than $170 billion this year. Schwab's margin loan balances rose 14% to $187.9 billion, including $60.7 billion tied to these strategies. Wurster gave no details or launch date, and the IRS has recently signalled interest in such products.
key_points: Schwab will launch a proprietary tax-aware long/short offering, per CEO Rick Wurster.
Schwab's margin loan balances rose 14% to $187.9 billion.
About $60.7 billion of margin lending is linked to tax-aware long/short strategies.
Assets in this category reportedly rose from $2 billion in 2022 to over $170 billion.

stories.story:
Charles Schwab's latest quarterly earnings drew attention to a figure in its margin lending data. Margin loan balances rose 14% quarter on quarter to $187.9 billion, and $60.7 billion of that was linked to tax-aware long/short strategies used by registered investment advisers. These strategies are designed to increase the number of losses available for harvesting by adding leverage on both long and short positions.

On the earnings call, CEO Rick Wurster told an analyst at UBS that the broker expects to launch its own version of the strategy. He said Schwab already offers direct indexing with strong tax-alpha results and that an extended long/short version would be a further way to generate revenue. He gave no timeline and few details, saying the firm would provide updates in future calls.

The category has grown quickly. Tax Alpha Insider estimated in September that assets had risen to more than $170 billion this year from about $2 billion in 2022. Analysts note the products carry relatively high fees and may attract wealthy clients, and that a Schwab version could lower typical account minimums. Open questions include whether the products would be restricted to Schwab advisers and platform users.

The approach is also drawing regulatory attention. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the IRS recently issued a notice about sophisticated ETF strategies used to shield capital gains, and it expressed interest in tax-aware structures. Law firm Ropes & Gray noted, however, that the notice does not treat tax-aware investing itself as a concern.
stories.market_take: A Schwab product in this category could add fee income, though no launch date has been set.

stories.headline: Munich dumps proprietary for open source (again) – but no Linux desktop
stories.claim: Munich is moving several infrastructure and collaboration systems from proprietary software to open source, though not returning to a Linux desktop.
stories.summary: At Open Source Summit Europe, Munich's chief digital officer Laura Dornheim said the city is replacing proprietary infrastructure with open-source tools rather than returning to a Linux desktop. Planned changes include replacing VMware with Proxmox, moving to OpenProject and XWiki, and adopting PostgreSQL. The city expects savings of roughly €1.5 million or more a year from the two infrastructure and collaboration migrations. The article recounts that Munich's earlier LiMux desktop project was ended for political reasons.
key_points: Munich is replacing VMware with Proxmox and Jira/Confluence with OpenProject and XWiki.
PostgreSQL is being adopted as an alternative to Oracle databases.
The two migrations are expected to save roughly €1.5 million or more annually.
The city's earlier LiMux Linux desktop was abandoned for political reasons, not technical ones, according to Dornheim.
Munich has set up an Open Source Program Office and embraces the public money, public code principle.
stories.story:
Munich, Germany's third-largest city, is shifting part of its public-sector IT away from proprietary software and towards open-source alternatives. Speaking at the Open Source Summit Europe in Prague, the city's chief digital officer, Laura Dornheim, said the city is not returning to the Linux desktop for now. Instead it is replacing individual layers of its software stack where a clear practical case exists. Examples include swapping VMware for Proxmox, moving from Jira and Confluence to OpenProject and XWiki, and adopting PostgreSQL in place of Oracle databases. Together the infrastructure and collaboration changes are expected to save about €1.5 million or more each year.

The article sets this against Munich's history. The city moved to the LiMux Linux desktop from 2003, completing the rollout by 2013 with more than 14,800 desktops. A later council, following the 2014 election, voted in 2017 to return to Windows. Dornheim argued that the reversal was driven by politics rather than technical failure, linking it to a deal in which Microsoft agreed to base its German headquarters in Munich.

Dornheim said open-source projects in the public sector need durable political backing and should be tied to priorities politicians understand, such as budgets and public services. The city has also created an Open Source Program Office and a public software portal, and shares tools such as the DAVe traffic-data application, which Wolfsburg has adopted. The article also notes that any cloud move to Azure would need assurances on GDPR compliance.

stories.claim: Anthropic is giving six METR evaluators employee-like access to its systems and will let them publish findings.
stories.summary: Anthropic has said it will give six evaluators from METR, a third-party nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, employee-like access to its hardware, office space and internal tools. METR will publish its findings, which Anthropic cannot withhold, though sensitive material may be redacted. The move follows a September proposal by CEO Dario Amodei for embedding outside evaluators. It comes as the FTC subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic over consumer harm concerns.
key_points: Six METR evaluators will get hardware, office space and internal tools roughly on par with Anthropic's risk teams.
METR can publish findings, and Anthropic cannot suppress them, though redactions may be requested.
The arrangement follows a September blog post by CEO Dario Amodei on third-party evaluators.
The FTC subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic over consumer harm the day before the article was written.
The federal framework remains largely voluntary, and the FRONTIER Act would require independent verification.
stories.story:
Anthropic has announced that it will give six evaluators from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, what it describes as employee-like access to its systems. The evaluators will receive Anthropic hardware and office space and can use internal tools broadly comparable to those used by the company's own risk assessment teams. Anthropic says it will encourage staff to share information with them, excluding a small set of categories such as customer data, privileged legal material and details of model architectures.

Under the arrangement, METR will publish its findings and Anthropic cannot withhold them. The company may ask METR to redact sensitive content. Anthropic argues it wants to be accountable but cannot share everything publicly, because some information could help malicious actors or is commercially sensitive. The company also stressed that evaluators such as METR do not hold equity in the firms they review, which it sees as a benefit. CEO Dario Amodei had proposed embedding outside evaluators in a September blog post.

The move comes amid debate over AI regulation in the United States. Federal rules under the Trump administration have so far mainly consisted of voluntary pledges, which are not binding. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act, introduced in July, would require certain AI firms to allow independent verification organisations to review their safety processes, and OpenAI has partly backed it. The article also reports that the FTC subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic and that the government said it would require AI companies to disclose safety incidents, after Anthropic reported that Claude had sent a false homicide tip to police. It remains unclear whether the announcement reflects existing plans or a response to the wider regulatory pressure.
stories.market_take: Stakeholders may see the voluntary access arrangement as a step toward tighter AI oversight, with limited direct effect on listed stocks.
